distractor_analysis.C: Performance portability is permitted under Standard III(D) when attribution, supporting records, and prior-firm credit are properly handled.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate performance reporting disclosures, composites, and simulated returns under Standard III(D)
question: A retail brokerage brochure prepared by Owen Carter, CFA, highlights a 12.4% five-year annualized return for its Managed Dividend Portfolio alongside a prominent statement: 'Outperformed the 10.8% benchmark return.' The 12.4% figure is calculated gross of the firm's 1.75% annual wrap fee, which would reduce net client returns to 10.65%—below the benchmark—yet the brochure fails to state whether returns are gross or net of fees. Carter has violated Standard III(D) by failing to:

options.A: Deduct federal capital gains taxes from the reported annual returns.
options.B: Clearly disclose that performance is presented gross of fees and accurately reflect the net impact on retail investors.
options.C: Limit marketing comparisons exclusively to money market index benchmarks.

explanation: Under Standard III(D) (Performance Presentation), members must ensure performance presentations are fair, accurate, and complete, which includes clearly disclosing whether performance is gross or net of management and trading fees. Presenting gross returns as 'outperformance' to fee-paying retail investors without disclosing the 1.75% fee that puts net returns below the benchmark is materially misleading.

distractor_analysis.A: After-tax presentation is optional unless specifically claimed; fee-basis disclosure (gross vs. net) is the critical omission here.
distractor_analysis.C: Using a relevant dividend equity benchmark is appropriate; the breach is hiding the gross-of-fee basis.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate performance reporting disclosures, composites, and simulated returns under Standard III(D)
question: During Q1 (January 1 through March 31), a new tactical currency strategy launched by Mei Lin, CFA, gains +7.5%. In her April marketing email to prospective institutional investors, Lin states: 'Our Global Currency Alpha Strategy is delivering a 33.5% annualized return in 2026.' She omits the three-month actual holding period and the compounding assumption. Lin's marketing email violates Standard III(D) because:

options.A: Currency strategies cannot report returns until completing a full three-year cycle.
options.B: She failed to compare the currency strategy against the S&P 500 Equity Index.
options.C: Annualizing a short three-month sub-period return misleads prospects by implying an unsustainable full-year return rate.

explanation: Under Standard III(D) (Performance Presentation), extrapolating or annualizing returns for periods shorter than one year—especially in volatile strategies like tactical currency trading—misleads prospective clients about expected full-year performance and violates the requirement for fair, accurate, and complete communication. Short-period results must be presented as unannualized cumulative returns for the exact stated period.

distractor_analysis.A: Short-period actual returns may be presented for the exact three-month window as unannualized returns.
distractor_analysis.B: Comparing a currency strategy to an unrelated equity index would worsen benchmark mismatch rather than fix annualization distortion.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate performance reporting disclosures, composites, and simulated returns under Standard III(D)
question: Crescent Wealth manages 32 discretionary balanced accounts following a uniform 60/40 model. Due to legacy low-basis stock holdings in one founder's account (#12), Account #12 returned 14.2% annually over three years while the asset-weighted average of all 32 accounts returned 9.6%. To simplify marketing materials, advisor Thomas Grant, CFA, prints only Account #12's 14.2% performance chart labeled 'Crescent Balanced Strategy Performance' without mentioning the other 31 accounts. Grant has violated Standard III(D) by:

options.A: Cherry-picking a single non-representative account without disclosing the composite performance of similarly managed accounts.
options.B: Refusing to force the founder of Account #12 to sell low-basis legacy equities.
options.C: Failing to obtain independent third-party GIPS verification before publishing any chart.

explanation: Under Standard III(D) (Performance Presentation), presenting a single best-performing account as representative of a strategy when all similarly managed accounts averaged 460 bps lower is deceptive and violates fair, accurate, and complete presentation. Recommended procedures call for presenting weighted-average composite performance of all similar portfolios rather than cherry-picked individual accounts.

distractor_analysis.B: Accommodating low-basis tax constraints in Account #12 is appropriate under Standard III(C); the breach is misrepresenting that account as typical.
distractor_analysis.C: GIPS verification is voluntary and not required to comply with Standard III(D).

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate performance reporting disclosures, composites, and simulated returns under Standard III(D)
question: Boutique investment advisor Kestrel Asset Management does not claim compliance with GIPS. When pitching a pension board, Kestrel presents a 7-year track record calculated as an asset-weighted composite of all actual fee-paying discretionary accounts in the strategy (including terminated accounts through termination), clearly discloses returns both gross and net of fees, uses a matching total-return benchmark, and notes full calculation methodology. Under Standard III(D), Kestrel's presentation is:

options.A: A violation, because claiming Standard III(D) compliance is impossible without full GIPS compliance.
options.B: A violation, because presenting both gross and net returns together creates ambiguity.
options.C: Compliant, because GIPS compliance is voluntary and Kestrel's presentation is fair, accurate, and complete.

explanation: Under Standard III(D) (Performance Presentation), GIPS compliance is strongly recommended as a voluntary best practice, NOT mandatory for compliance with Standard III(D). A non-GIPS firm complies fully with Standard III(D) when it presents fair, accurate, and complete performance using asset-weighted composites of all actual similar accounts (including terminated accounts), clear gross/net fee disclosures, and an appropriate benchmark.

distractor_analysis.A: GIPS is strictly voluntary; Standard III(D) can be satisfied through transparent, complete non-GIPS composite disclosures.
distractor_analysis.B: Showing both gross and net returns side by side enhances transparency rather than creating ambiguity.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate performance reporting disclosures, composites, and simulated returns under Standard III(D)
question: Portfolio manager Lucas Moreno, CFA, runs an Emerging Market High-Yield Corporate Debt Fund (average credit rating B+, effective duration 5.5 years). In client factsheets, Moreno exclusively compares his fund's 8.9% annualized return against the 3-month US Treasury Bill Index (2.1%) and highlights '+680 bps alpha.' Moreno's benchmark selection most directly violates Standard III(D) because:

options.A: Treasury bill indices are prohibited from all fixed-income marketing materials.
options.B: Comparing a high-risk emerging-market credit fund solely against a risk-free cash index misrepresents risk-adjusted skill and value added.
options.C: High-yield funds must compare returns solely against equity benchmarks such as the MSCI Emerging Markets Index.

explanation: Under Standard III(D) (Performance Presentation), fair and complete performance reporting requires comparing portfolio returns against a relevant benchmark matching the strategy's asset class, credit risk, geography, and duration. Claiming '+680 bps alpha' over risk-free 3-month T-bills while omitting an emerging-market high-yield bond benchmark misleads clients regarding risk-adjusted outperformance.

distractor_analysis.A: Cash indices are acceptable for money-market mandates or as a secondary risk-free reference, not as the sole benchmark for risky credit.
distractor_analysis.C: A bond fund should be benchmarked against a comparable fixed-income/credit index, not an equity index.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Determine appropriate handling of confidential current, former, and prospective client information under Standard III(E)
question: Two years after high-net-worth client Dr. Arthur Vance transfers all his accounts away from Meridian Private Wealth to a competitor, a financial journalist contacts Meridian advisor Nora Gallagher, CFA, to verify rumors about Dr. Vance's past portfolio losses and asset size during a public business dispute. Dr. Vance has not authorized any release, and no subpoena exists. Gallagher confirms Dr. Vance's historical account balance to 'set the record straight.' Gallagher has:

options.A: Violated Standard III(E) (Preservation of Confidentiality), because confidentiality obligations survive indefinitely after the client relationship ends.
options.B: Complied with Standard III(E), because Dr. Vance ceased to be a client two years earlier.
options.C: Complied with Standard III(E), provided she only disclosed historical figures rather than current holdings.

explanation: Under Standard III(E) (Preservation of Confidentiality), members must keep information about current, former, and prospective clients strictly confidential unless the client permits disclosure, disclosure is required by law, or the information concerns illegal activities by the client. The duty of confidentiality persists indefinitely even after a client terminates the relationship.

distractor_analysis.B: Former clients remain explicitly protected under Standard III(E) after terminating advisory relationships.
distractor_analysis.C: Historical balances and performance remain confidential client data protected under Standard III(E).

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Determine appropriate handling of confidential current, former, and prospective client information under Standard III(E)
question: While reviewing wire transfer logs for a private client account, compliance analyst Devon Patel, CFA, uncovers clear documentary evidence that the client is structuring fragmented cash deposits across shell companies to launder proceeds from illegal narcotics trafficking. Patel alerts the firm's Chief Compliance Officer and outside legal counsel, who instruct Patel to file a Suspicious Activity Report with financial crime authorities without notifying the client. Patel's disclosure to authorities is:

options.A: A violation of Standard III(E), because client permission was not obtained prior to external reporting.
options.B: Permissible under Standard III(E), which provides an explicit exception for information concerning illegal client activities and disclosures required by law.
options.C: A violation of Standard III(E), unless a judge first issues a criminal conviction.

explanation: Under Standard III(E) (Preservation of Confidentiality), confidentiality is overridden when (1) the information concerns illegal activities on the part of the client or prospective client, or (2) disclosure is required by applicable law (such as anti-money-laundering statutes). Consulting legal/compliance counsel and reporting suspected money laundering to proper authorities complies fully with Standard III(E).

distractor_analysis.A: Standard III(E) does not require client consent when illegal client activity or statutory reporting mandates apply.
distractor_analysis.C: Reasonable evidence of illegal activity and mandatory statutory AML reporting trigger the exception prior to any court conviction.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Determine appropriate handling of confidential current, former, and prospective client information under Standard III(E)
question: The CFA Institute Professional Conduct Program (PCP) initiates an investigation into alleged front-running by a colleague at Apex Investments and formally requests trading blotters and client allocation logs containing client names and account details from portfolio manager Grace Yoon, CFA. Without obtaining prior permission from each individual client, Yoon supplies the requested records directly to the PCP. Has Yoon violated Standard III(E)?

options.A: Yes, because CFA Institute is a private professional organization rather than a government regulator.
options.B: Yes, unless she first redacts every client name and account identifier.
options.C: No, because Standard III(E) permits sharing confidential client information with the CFA Institute Professional Conduct Program during an investigation.

explanation: Under the Standard III(E) (Preservation of Confidentiality) guidance, members and candidates are expressly permitted to cooperate with the CFA Institute Professional Conduct Program (PCP) and submit confidential client information requested during a PCP inquiry without violating Standard III(E), as the PCP itself maintains strict confidentiality over investigative records.

distractor_analysis.A: Although PCP is not a government agency, the Standards explicitly carve out cooperation with PCP investigations.
distractor_analysis.B: Unredacted records may be provided directly to PCP staff when needed to verify allocation fairness or misconduct.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Determine appropriate handling of confidential current, former, and prospective client information under Standard III(E)
question: To win a major endowment mandate, institutional sales director Marcus Reed, CFA, includes a slide in his RFP pitchbook listing the names and approximate asset sizes of six prestigious Fortune 500 corporate pension plans that his firm currently manages. Although the figures are generally positive and two of those pensions publicly announce their managers in annual filings, Reed did not ask any of the six clients for permission to use their names as marketing references. Reed has violated Standard III(E) because:

options.A: Client identities and relationship details are confidential and cannot be disclosed for marketing without explicit prior client permission.
options.B: Corporate pension plans may never be used as marketing references even with written consent.
options.C: Standard III(E) applies only to individual retail clients, not institutional pension plans.

explanation: Under Standard III(E) (Preservation of Confidentiality), even the fact that an organization or individual is a client—along with account sizes—is confidential client information. Using current client names as marketing references in an RFP without obtaining prior client permission (unless already unmistakably public and approved, or better yet with explicit written consent) violates Standard III(E).

distractor_analysis.B: Clients may be listed as references if they grant explicit prior permission.
distractor_analysis.C: Standard III(E) protects institutional, corporate, and individual current, former, and prospective clients equally.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Determine appropriate handling of confidential current, former, and prospective client information under Standard III(E)
question: Preparing for client review meetings, associate advisor Priya Nair, CFA, pastes an unredacted spreadsheet containing 35 high-net-worth clients' full names, tax identification numbers, net worth figures, and current portfolio holdings into a free, public web-based generative AI chatbot to draft personalized meeting summaries. The AI vendor's terms state uploaded prompts may be stored and used for model training. Nair's action most directly violates:

options.A: Standard V(A) only, because generative AI outputs lack a reasonable basis.
options.B: Standard III(D) only, because meeting summaries omit GIPS disclosures.
options.C: Standard III(E) (Preservation of Confidentiality), by exposing private client data to an unauthorized external system.

explanation: Under Standard III(E) (Preservation of Confidentiality), members must safeguard client data from unauthorized electronic access or third-party exposure. Uploading non-public client identities, tax IDs, and holdings to an unapproved public generative AI platform that retains inputs breaches client confidentiality. Recommended procedures require strict cybersecurity controls, approved enterprise-isolated tools, or complete anonymization before any external processing.

distractor_analysis.A: While AI tools require diligence under V(A) if used for research, the immediate breach here is leaking PII and holdings under III(E).
distractor_analysis.B: Meeting summaries are not composite performance advertisements under Standard III(D).

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Determine appropriate handling of confidential current, former, and prospective client information under Standard III(E)
question: Wealth advisor Henrik Solberg, CFA, manages two separate individual accounts at his firm: an Individual Retirement Account solely in Husband's name and a separate individual brokerage account solely in Wife's name. Neither spouse holds trading authority or written view-access on the other's individual account. Amid contentious divorce proceedings, Wife calls Solberg asking for the current balance and recent withdrawal history of Husband's IRA. Solberg should:

options.A: Provide the balance because spouses share marital property rights by default.
options.B: Refuse to disclose Husband's account details unless Husband provides explicit authorization or a valid court order/subpoena requires disclosure.
options.C: Disclose only the total account balance without listing specific security holdings.

explanation: Under Standard III(E) (Preservation of Confidentiality), each individual client account is protected against unauthorized third-party disclosure—even to a spouse who lacks formal account authorization or power of attorney. Solberg must withhold Husband's private account details unless Husband consents in writing or disclosure is legally compelled via a valid subpoena or court order.

distractor_analysis.A: Marital property laws in divorce do not authorize an advisor to breach account-level confidentiality absent consent or a court order.
distractor_analysis.C: Revealing even the aggregate account balance or withdrawal status without permission violates Standard III(E).

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Determine appropriate handling of confidential current, former, and prospective client information under Standard III(E)
question: A sovereign wealth fund invites three asset managers, including Horizon Capital, to participate in a closed request-for-proposal (RFP) process and shares confidential internal asset-liability mismatch projections and upcoming currency hedging targets. Horizon does not win the mandate. Two months later, Horizon portfolio manager Samuel Kim, CFA, shares the sovereign fund's proprietary hedging targets with a competing institutional prospect to demonstrate Horizon's market insight. Kim has violated Standard III(E) because:

options.A: Prospective clients are covered by Standard III(E) confidentiality protections even when no formal advisory contract is ultimately signed.
options.B: Sovereign wealth funds require diplomatic immunity waivers before RFP discussions.
options.C: Horizon cannot discuss currency hedging strategies with any institutional prospect.

explanation: Standard III(E) (Preservation of Confidentiality) explicitly protects current, former, AND prospective clients. Confidential strategic, financial, or portfolio data shared by a prospective client during an RFP or pitch remains strictly protected even if the prospect never hires the firm. Disclosing those private hedging plans to another prospect violates Standard III(E).

distractor_analysis.B: Protection arises directly from Standard III(E)'s coverage of prospective clients, not diplomatic immunity.
distractor_analysis.C: Horizon may discuss its own general hedging capabilities, but never another prospect's confidential data.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Apply Standard IV(A) Loyalty to situations involving departing an employer, independent practice, and whistleblowing
question: Two weeks before submitting his resignation from Northstar Capital to join a competing hedge fund, senior equity analyst Nathan Brooks, CFA, downloads Northstar's proprietary discounted cash flow valuation templates—which Brooks personally programmed during company hours—and exports Northstar's confidential client contact CRM spreadsheet onto a personal encrypted USB drive. Under Standard IV(A), Brooks's conduct is:

options.A: Compliant with respect to the DCF templates because Brooks authored them himself.
options.B: Compliant provided he waits until after his final workday to open the USB files.
options.C: A violation, because proprietary models created on employer time and confidential client lists belong strictly to the employer.

explanation: Under Standard IV(A) (Loyalty), employees must not misappropriate employer property, trade secrets, or confidential client lists upon departure. Models, software, and research created on the employer's time and resources are firm property (also reinforced by Standard V(C)), even if developed personally by the departing employee. Taking them via USB without written employer authorization violates Standard IV(A).

distractor_analysis.A: Work product developed during employment belongs to the employer, not the individual creator, absent an explicit contrary contract.
distractor_analysis.B: Misappropriating firm property and client lists prior to resignation violates loyalty regardless of when the USB is later opened.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Apply Standard IV(A) Loyalty to situations involving departing an employer, independent practice, and whistleblowing
question: Portfolio manager Claire Beaumont, CFA, plans to resign from Apex Wealth in two months to launch an independent registered investment advisor. On Saturday mornings using her personal laptop at home, Beaumont drafts articles of incorporation, leases an empty office suite, and sets up a business checking account. She performs all current Apex duties diligently, takes zero Apex files, and makes no contact with Apex clients or coworkers about her plans. Beaumont's actions are:

options.A: Compliant with Standard IV(A), because reasonable personal-time preparations to establish a new business do not breach loyalty if current duties and employer assets are respected.
options.B: A violation of Standard IV(A), because any step toward creating a competing business while still employed breaches loyalty.
options.C: A violation of Standard IV(A), unless she first receives written permission from Apex's CEO before leasing office space.

explanation: Under Standard IV(A) (Loyalty), making reasonable preparations to leave and start a competing enterprise—such as incorporating an entity, retaining legal counsel, or leasing space on personal time—is permissible so long as the employee does not solicit clients or staff before departure, misappropriate firm IP/records, misuse employer time/equipment, or breach a valid employment covenant.

distractor_analysis.B: Passive off-hours logistical preparations without solicitation or IP theft do not violate Standard IV(A).
distractor_analysis.C: Employer consent is required for active independent practice while employed, not for private off-hours preparations to depart.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Apply Standard IV(A) Loyalty to situations involving departing an employer, independent practice, and whistleblowing
question: After resigning cleanly from Vanguardia Advisors—leaving behind all files, models, and client lists—wealth advisor Mateo Silva, CFA, launches his own advisory boutique. Because Silva signed no non-compete or non-solicitation agreement, once his resignation is effective he searches public LinkedIn profiles and telephone directories to locate former clients whose names he remembers and sends them an announcement introducing his new firm. Silva has:

options.A: Violated Standard IV(A), because former employees may never contact former clients regardless of how contact info is obtained.
options.B: Complied with Standard IV(A), because contacting former clients post-departure using memory and public sources—absent a binding non-compete—does not breach employer loyalty.
options.C: Violated Standard III(E), because remembering a former client's name breaches confidentiality.

explanation: Under Standard IV(A) (Loyalty), once an employee's resignation is effective and assuming no valid non-solicitation/non-compete agreement bars contact, reaching out to former clients using publicly available directories or unassisted memory—without having taken proprietary firm client lists or solicited clients before resigning—does not violate Standard IV(A).

distractor_analysis.A: Pre-departure solicitation and stolen client lists are barred, not post-departure outreach via public directories when no contractual restriction exists.
distractor_analysis.C: Contacting a former client directly to offer services does not disclose confidential data to third parties under Standard III(E).

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Apply Standard IV(A) Loyalty to situations involving departing an employer, independent practice, and whistleblowing
question: Full-time fixed-income analyst Julian Park, CFA, works at a large institutional asset manager that serves only pension funds. To earn extra income on weekends, Park launches a paid personal financial planning consultancy advising individual retail physicians for a 2,500 USD annual retainer. Reasoning that his weekend retail clients do not overlap with his employer's institutional pension clients, Park does not notify his employer. Park has violated Standard IV(A) because:

options.A: Analysts may never perform any outside financial work, even with employer written consent.
options.B: Charging 2,500 USD retainers exceeds CFA Institute fee guidelines.
options.C: Engaging in independent practice for compensation requires prior written notice and written consent from the employer.

explanation: Under Standard IV(A) (Loyalty), members must not engage in independent practice for compensation that could compete with or interfere with their employer unless they provide written notification detailing the nature, duration, and compensation of the services and obtain WRITTEN CONSENT from their employer beforehand. Even non-overlapping paid financial advisory work carries regulatory, liability, and time-allocation implications requiring employer consent.

distractor_analysis.A: Independent practice is permitted once full written disclosure and written employer consent are obtained.
distractor_analysis.B: CFA Institute sets no fixed fee cap on financial planning retainers.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Apply Standard IV(A) Loyalty to situations involving departing an employer, independent practice, and whistleblowing
question: Compliance associate Fiona Byrne, CFA, discovers that her firm's Chief Investment Officer has been deliberately falsifying third-party price quotes on illiquid private debt holdings to inflate fund NAV and earn higher incentive fees. After escalating the evidence internally to the Board Audit Committee and being told to 'drop the matter immediately,' Byrne reports the valuation fraud confidentially to the national securities commission—triggering regulatory sanctions that severely damage her employer's stock price. Under Standard IV(A), Byrne's whistleblowing is:

options.A: A violation of Standard IV(A), because employees may never take external action that harms their employer's financial standing.
options.B: Compliant with Standard IV(A), because loyalty to employer never supersedes protecting client interests, legal compliance, and market integrity.
options.C: A violation of Standard III(E), because reporting firm fraud discloses fund holdings to regulators.

explanation: Under Standard IV(A) (Loyalty), the duty of loyalty to an employer does not require participating in or concealing illegal or unethical behavior. Whistleblowing—disclosing employer misconduct to regulatory authorities to protect clients and capital market integrity, rather than for personal gain—is explicitly permitted and does not violate Standard IV(A).

distractor_analysis.A: Loyalty to employer is subordinate to client protection, law, and market integrity; covering up fraud is never required.
distractor_analysis.C: Standard III(E) explicitly permits disclosures required by law or involving illegal activities.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Apply Standard IV(A) Loyalty to situations involving departing an employer, independent practice, and whistleblowing
question: While still employed as lead portfolio manager at Sterling Partners, Omar Hassan, CFA, meets privately for lunch with three institutional client trustees and two junior analysts from his team. During the meeting, Hassan explains that he plans to resign next month to open a competing boutique and asks both the trustees to sign non-binding letters of intent to transfer 200 million USD and the analysts to commit to joining him. Hassan has violated:

options.A: Standard IV(A) (Loyalty), by actively soliciting employer clients and staff while still employed.
options.B: Standard IV(B) only, because he paid for lunch without written HR approval.
options.C: No standard, because the letters of intent are non-binding.

explanation: Under Standard IV(A) (Loyalty), until resignation becomes effective, an employee must act strictly in the employer's best interest. Actively soliciting current clients to transfer assets or recruiting coworkers to leave while still on the employer's payroll directly deprives the employer of business and violates Standard IV(A), regardless of whether letters are non-binding.

distractor_analysis.B: Paying for lunch is not the issue; pre-departure client and employee solicitation breaches loyalty.
distractor_analysis.C: Solicitation itself while employed violates Standard IV(A), even before binding contracts are signed.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Apply Standard IV(A) Loyalty to situations involving departing an employer, independent practice, and whistleblowing
question: Meridian Asset Management enforces a strict written compliance policy prohibiting employees from posting specific stock opinions or buy/sell commentary on external internet forums or social media without pre-clearance. Junior analyst Trevor Bell, CFA, uses an anonymous handle on a public investment forum during weekends to post detailed Buy recommendations on three mid-cap stocks he does not own personally and his firm does not cover. Bell's posts violate Standard IV(A) primarily because:

options.A: Anonymous social media handles automatically violate Standard VII(B).
options.B: Mid-cap stock analysis requires a minimum five-year track record.
options.C: Violating an employer's reasonable compliance policies breaches the duty of loyalty, even if no client suffered direct financial loss.

explanation: Under Standard IV(A) (Loyalty), members must comply with all reasonable employer compliance policies and supervisory directives designed to protect the firm's regulatory standing and reputation. Deliberately circumventing firm social-media pre-clearance rules exposes the employer to regulatory risk and violates Standard IV(A), even without personal holdings or direct client harm.

distractor_analysis.A: Standard VII(B) governs references to CFA Institute/designation, not anonymous stock commentary.
distractor_analysis.B: No five-year track record is needed to analyze mid-cap equities.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Apply Standard IV(A) Loyalty to situations involving departing an employer, independent practice, and whistleblowing
question: Equity strategist Rachel Kim, CFA, is asked to serve as the unpaid volunteer treasurer for a local community animal shelter. The shelter keeps its modest operating reserves strictly in insured bank checking accounts, receives zero investment advisory services from Kim's employer, and requires only three hours of Kim's time on Sunday afternoons. Kim does not obtain formal written consent from her employer's compliance office (assuming employer policy does not require reporting unpaid civic roles). Under Standard IV(A), Kim's volunteer work is:

options.A: Compliant, because unpaid civic volunteer work that neither competes with nor interferes with employer duties does not constitute independent practice for compensation.
options.B: A violation of Standard IV(A), because all volunteer board or treasurer roles require written employer consent.
options.C: A violation of Standard IV(B), because the shelter benefits economically from Kim's financial expertise.

explanation: Under Standard IV(A) (Loyalty), written notice and employer consent are required for independent practice undertaken FOR COMPENSATION or activities that compete with or interfere with the employer's business. Unpaid community volunteer work on weekends that involves no compensation, no overlapping client/investment business, and no interference with work duties does not violate Standard IV(A).

distractor_analysis.B: Absent a specific firm policy requiring disclosure of all civic roles, unpaid non-competing volunteerism does not violate IV(A).
distractor_analysis.C: Standard IV(B) restricts receiving competing/conflicting compensation, not providing unpaid charity service.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Apply Standard IV(A) Loyalty to situations involving departing an employer, independent practice, and whistleblowing
question: After giving two weeks' notice of resignation to accept a role elsewhere, derivatives trader Daniel Cho, CFA, stops monitoring intraday client option margin alerts during his final eight business days, causing two client accounts to suffer forced liquidation penalties and exposing his employer to client reimbursement claims. Cho's deliberate neglect during his notice period violates:

options.A: Standard VII(A) only, because his behavior undermines the CFA exam.
options.B: Standard IV(A) (Loyalty), because an employee owes full diligence and skills to the employer until employment formally ends.
options.C: No standard, because submitting resignation notice terminates operational loyalty obligations.

explanation: Under Standard IV(A) (Loyalty), members must not deprive their employer of the advantage of their skills and abilities or cause harm to the employer until their employment relationship actually terminates. Neglecting assigned risk-monitoring duties during a two-week notice period harms both clients and the employer, violating Standard IV(A) (and III(A)).

distractor_analysis.A: Standard VII(A) governs participation in CFA Institute programs/exams, not workplace trading negligence.
distractor_analysis.C: Notice period employment remains full employment; duties continue until the final effective departure date.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Apply Standard IV(A) Loyalty to situations involving departing an employer, independent practice, and whistleblowing
question: During an alumni dinner, quantitative analyst Priya Kapoor, CFA, shares the proprietary Python risk-factor weighting code used by her employer's flagship market-neutral hedge fund with a former classmate who runs a competing fund, in exchange for industry gossip about upcoming analyst layoffs. Kapoor's disclosure violates Standard IV(A) primarily because she:

options.A: Attended a social dinner with employees of a competing asset manager.
options.B: Failed to verify whether the classmate holds the CFA charter.
options.C: Divulged her employer's confidential proprietary intellectual property to a competitor.

explanation: Under Standard IV(A) (Loyalty), members must safeguard employer trade secrets, proprietary software, research models, and confidential business information. Sharing proprietary factor-weighting code with a competitor directly undermines the employer's competitive advantage and violates Standard IV(A).

distractor_analysis.A: Socializing with industry peers is completely normal when confidential firm information is protected.
distractor_analysis.B: Divulging employer trade secrets is prohibited regardless of whether the recipient holds the CFA charter.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate gifts, outside compensation, and written consent requirements under Standard IV(B)
question: A wealthy individual client tells his portfolio manager, Arthur Novak, CFA, that if his account beats the Russell 1000 Index by more than 250 basis points this year, the client will personally wire Novak a 30,000 USD cash bonus and give him free use of a Swiss ski chalet for two weeks. Novak mentions the offer to his branch manager over coffee, who verbally replies, 'Sure, go ahead—keep the client happy.' Novak accepts the arrangement. Novak has violated Standard IV(B) because he failed to:

options.A: Obtain prior written consent from all parties involved—both his employer and the client.
options.B: Share 50% of the 30,000 USD cash bonus with his branch manager.
options.C: Guarantee the 250 bps outperformance in writing to the client.

explanation: Under Standard IV(B) (Additional Compensation Arrangements), members must not accept gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration that competes with or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with their employer's interest unless they obtain WRITTEN CONSENT from ALL parties involved (here, written approval from both the employer/compliance and the client offering the arrangement). Verbal approval from a branch manager is insufficient.

distractor_analysis.B: Splitting an undisclosed or verbally approved outside bonus does not satisfy Standard IV(B)'s written-consent rule.
distractor_analysis.C: Guaranteeing market outperformance violates Standard I(C) (Misrepresentation) and Standard III(D).

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate gifts, outside compensation, and written consent requirements under Standard IV(B)
question: Technology equity analyst Sofia Lin, CFA, is invited to join the paid advisory board of a private artificial-intelligence startup not currently covered by her brokerage firm, earning 20,000 USD worth of startup stock options annually. Lin signs the advisory board contract on Monday and sends an email to her firm's HR director on Friday informing HR of her new board role. Has Lin complied with Standard IV(B)?

options.A: Yes, because the startup is private and outside her firm's current coverage universe.
options.B: No, because she failed to obtain written consent from all parties BEFORE entering into the compensation arrangement.
options.C: Yes, because disclosing by email within five business days satisfies post-event reporting rules.

explanation: Under Standard IV(B) (Additional Compensation Arrangements), written consent from all parties involved (employer and the outside party) must be obtained PRIOR to accepting or entering into the additional compensation arrangement—not retroactively after signing the contract. Even if the startup is not currently covered, future coverage or IPO underwriting conflicts could arise.

distractor_analysis.A: Potential future conflicts and time/reputational commitments make prior written consent mandatory even for uncovered private entities.
distractor_analysis.C: Standard IV(B) requires prior written consent, not post-signing email notification.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate gifts, outside compensation, and written consent requirements under Standard IV(B)
question: Quantitative researcher Marcus Chen, CFA, is offered an adjunct lecturing position to teach a graduate fixed-income seminar one evening per week for a 9,000 USD semester stipend. Before accepting, Chen writes to his employer's Chief Compliance Officer detailing the teaching schedule, curriculum, and 9,000 USD stipend, and writes to the university dean confirming his full-time asset-management employment. After receiving formal written email approval from both his CCO and the university, Chen signs the teaching contract. Chen's actions are:

options.A: A violation of Standard IV(B), because outside income above 5,000 USD is strictly prohibited.
options.B: A violation of Standard IV(A), because academic lecturing competes with asset management.
options.C: Compliant with Standard IV(B) (and IV(A)), because he disclosed all terms and obtained prior written consent from all parties involved.

explanation: Under Standard IV(B) (Additional Compensation Arrangements), verifiable electronic communications such as formal email constitute 'written consent.' By disclosing the nature, duration, and dollar amount of the compensation and receiving prior written approval from all parties involved (both his employer's CCO and the university), Chen fully complied with Standard IV(B) and Standard IV(A).

distractor_analysis.A: Standard IV(B) sets no absolute dollar ceiling once proper written consent is secured.
distractor_analysis.B: Evening university lecturing approved in writing by the employer does not breach employer loyalty.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate gifts, outside compensation, and written consent requirements under Standard IV(B)
question: Financial advisor Kevin Walsh, CFA, works at a registered broker-dealer whose standard payout grid pays 0.50% across all private placements. An external private-credit fund sponsor privately offers to pay Walsh personally an extra 1.25% cash marketing fee directly into his personal bank account for every client dollar he places into their new fund. Walsh agrees and promotes the fund heavily to clients without informing his firm or clients. Walsh has violated:

options.A: Standard IV(B) (Additional Compensation Arrangements), as well as Standards I(B) and VI(A), by accepting undisclosed conflicting compensation.
options.B: Standard V(C) only, because private credit funds lack sufficient historical records.
options.C: No standard, provided the private-credit fund matches each client's risk tolerance.

explanation: Accepting an undisclosed 1.25% direct cash kickback from an external sponsor competes directly with the employer's compensation structure and creates severe bias in product selection. This violates Standard IV(B) (requiring written consent from all parties), Standard I(B) (Independence and Objectivity), and Standard VI(A) (Disclosure of Conflicts).

distractor_analysis.B: The core ethical breaches are secret third-party compensation and severe conflicts of interest, not record retention.
distractor_analysis.C: Suitability never excuses taking secret third-party cash incentives without employer and client written consent/disclosure.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate gifts, outside compensation, and written consent requirements under Standard IV(B)
question: Two years prior to joining Horizon Investments as a senior technology portfolio manager, Hannah Diaz, CFA, entered a multi-year consulting agreement paying her 18,000 USD annually to advise an enterprise cloud vendor on capital allocation. Upon starting at Horizon, Diaz assumes she does not need to mention the consulting arrangement because it predated her employment at Horizon and involves no stock ownership. Diaz has violated Standard IV(B) because:

options.A: Software consulting agreements are permanently forbidden for CFA charterholders.
options.B: Pre-existing outside compensation arrangements that could conflict with new employer duties must be disclosed to obtain written consent upon joining.
options.C: Standard IV(B) applies only if the arrangement pays stock rather than cash.

explanation: Under Standard IV(B) (Additional Compensation Arrangements), members joining a new employer must disclose all pre-existing ongoing outside compensation arrangements that might reasonably conflict with or affect their duties to the new employer (such as consulting for a tech vendor Horizon could invest in) and obtain written consent from all parties to continue.

distractor_analysis.A: Consulting is permitted if disclosed and consented to in writing by all involved parties.
distractor_analysis.C: Cash retainers, royalties, equity options, and non-cash benefits are all covered equally by Standard IV(B).

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate gifts, outside compensation, and written consent requirements under Standard IV(B)
question: Which of the following client gestures most clearly triggers Standard IV(B) (Additional Compensation Arrangements) requiring prior written consent from all parties involved, rather than falling solely under routine gift policies under Standard I(B)?

options.A: A long-standing client sends a 55 USD seasonal fruit basket to the advisor's office at year-end with a thank-you card.
options.B: A client invites the advisor to a local 75 USD lunch meeting to review annual tax-loss harvesting.
options.C: A client promises to pay for an all-expenses-paid 10-day European yacht trip for the advisor's family if the portfolio ends the year positive.

explanation: Standard IV(B) targets outside compensation, gifts, or benefits that compete with or create a conflict with the employer's interest—particularly contingent performance incentives or lavish benefits tied to portfolio results, which require written consent from all parties involved. Modest customary tokens like a 55 USD holiday fruit basket or a 75 USD working lunch fall under Standard I(B) gift/hospitality policies and do not require formal multi-party written contracts.

distractor_analysis.A: A modest 55 USD holiday gift unrelated to future performance does not constitute an additional compensation arrangement under IV(B).
distractor_analysis.B: A routine 75 USD business lunch falls under ordinary client hospitality rather than contingent outside compensation.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate gifts, outside compensation, and written consent requirements under Standard IV(B)
question: Equity research analyst Lucas Bennett, CFA, receives an offer from an independent financial newsletter publisher to write paid weekend equity commentary for 1,200 USD per article. Bennett submits a written request outlining the topic scope, time commitment, and pay to his employer's compliance department. Compliance denies the request in writing due to potential reputational and coverage overlap risks. Bennett emails the publisher declining the offer. Bennett has:

options.A: Violated Standard IV(B), because his employer unreasonably restricted his weekend earnings.
options.B: Complied fully with Standard IV(B) by seeking prior written consent and declining the outside arrangement once consent was refused.
options.C: Violated Standard IV(A), because merely asking to write external commentary shows disloyalty.

explanation: Under Standard IV(B) (Additional Compensation Arrangements), requesting written consent before entering an external arrangement and respecting the employer's written refusal by declining the offer demonstrates textbook compliance. Asking compliance for review is encouraged and never breaches loyalty.

distractor_analysis.A: Employers have the legitimate right to withhold consent for external financial commentary that creates coverage or reputational conflict.
distractor_analysis.C: Transparently requesting permission from compliance adheres to Standards IV(A) and IV(B).

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Assess supervisory adequacy, delegation, enforcement, and escalation duties under Standard IV(C)
question: While reviewing daily order audit logs, Chief Equity Trader Samuel Ortiz, CFA, discovers that a junior trader under his direct supervision repeatedly delayed submitting large pension buy orders by 15 minutes in order to buy shares in his own personal account first. Ortiz calls the trader into his office, warns him verbally never to do it again, and leaves the trader on the desk with full trading privileges without alerting compliance or auditing prior months' trades. Ortiz has violated Standard IV(C) because:

options.A: Upon detecting a violation, a supervisor must initiate a thorough investigation, place appropriate limits on the wrongdoer, and escalate rather than issuing an informal verbal warning.
options.B: Standard IV(C) requires supervisors to physically execute every trade personally.
options.C: Front-running only violates Standard IV(C) if the pension client files a formal lawsuit.

explanation: Under Standard IV(C) (Responsibilities of Supervisors), detecting a violation triggers an affirmative duty to respond promptly: the supervisor must conduct or initiate a thorough investigation (including past activity), place heightened supervision or operational limits on the employee pending investigation, escalate to compliance/senior management, and enforce discipline. A private verbal warning with zero monitoring or escalation fails Standard IV(C).

distractor_analysis.B: Supervisors may delegate execution and rely on reasonable supervisory systems, provided violations are rigorously investigated and controlled.
distractor_analysis.C: Supervisory accountability does not wait for external client lawsuits.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Assess supervisory adequacy, delegation, enforcement, and escalation duties under Standard IV(C)
question: Horizon Asset Management operates a robust compliance infrastructure featuring comprehensive written policies, mandatory quarterly ethics training, automated pre-clearance software, duplicate broker feeds, and annual signed compliance attestations. Despite these enforced controls, a rogue analyst secretly opens a brokerage account under a distant cousin's name using forged identity papers and front-runs a firm upgrade. Under Standard IV(C), the analyst's supervisor has:

options.A: Violated Standard IV(C) strictly on a no-fault basis because a violation occurred within her department.
options.B: Violated Standard IV(C) unless she personally inspects every employee's private tax returns.
options.C: Not violated Standard IV(C), because supervisors are held to making reasonable efforts rather than guaranteeing total prevention of deliberate, hidden fraud.

explanation: Under Standard IV(C) (Responsibilities of Supervisors), supervisors must make REASONABLE efforts to prevent and detect violations through adequate compliance systems and active enforcement. Standard IV(C) does not impose strict vicarious liability when a well-designed, actively enforced compliance system is deliberately circumvented by a rogue employee falsifying records.

distractor_analysis.A: Standard IV(C) imposes a 'reasonable efforts' standard, not strict no-fault liability for hidden fraud.
distractor_analysis.B: Inspecting personal tax returns is neither required nor standard when automated feeds, attestations, and surveillance operate properly.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Assess supervisory adequacy, delegation, enforcement, and escalation duties under Standard IV(C)
question: Branch Manager Elena Kovalenko, CFA, oversees six wealth advisors, two of whom are neither CFA charterholders nor candidates in the CFA Program. One non-CFA advisor distributes unapproved marketing flyers guaranteeing 12% annual returns. When questioned by regulators, Kovalenko argues she had no CFA Code obligation to monitor that advisor because he is not subject to the CFA Institute Code and Standards. Kovalenko's argument is flawed under Standard IV(C) because:

options.A: Standard IV(C) only covers marketing employees who hold FINRA licenses.
options.B: Supervisory responsibility extends to anyone subject to the member's supervision or authority, regardless of whether those subordinates are CFA members or candidates.
options.C: Non-CFA subordinates are governed exclusively by Standard I(A).

explanation: Standard IV(C) (Responsibilities of Supervisors) explicitly requires members and candidates to make reasonable efforts to ensure that ANYONE subject to their supervision or authority—whether CFA charterholders, candidates, non-CFA advisors, traders, or support staff—complies with applicable laws, rules, regulations, and ethical standards.

distractor_analysis.A: Supervisory duties cover all supervised personnel regardless of license type or CFA affiliation.
distractor_analysis.C: Subordinates' legal duties under I(A) do not relieve a CFA supervisor of oversight accountability under IV(C).

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Assess supervisory adequacy, delegation, enforcement, and escalation duties under Standard IV(C)
question: Head of Research Martin Vogel, CFA, delegates daily compliance pre-publication review of equity reports to a senior vice president. Over six months, the senior VP routinely approves analyst drafts in under two minutes without checking sources or conflict disclosures, and Vogel never reviews the VP's sign-off logs. An analyst subsequently publishes a report containing fabricated channel checks. Under Standard IV(C), Vogel:

options.A: Violated Standard IV(C), because delegating supervisory tasks does not absolve the supervisor of ultimate responsibility to verify the delegate performs adequately.
options.B: Complied with Standard IV(C) because he delegated the task to a senior officer.
options.C: Violated Standard IV(C) only if Vogel personally co-authored the fabricated report.

explanation: Under Standard IV(C) (Responsibilities of Supervisors), a member may delegate day-to-day supervisory tasks to qualified subordinates, but CANNOT delegate away ultimate supervisory responsibility. A supervisor must monitor delegates periodically to confirm compliance reviews are thorough and effective; failing to oversee a rubber-stamping delegate breaches Standard IV(C).

distractor_analysis.B: Delegation without ongoing oversight fails the 'reasonable efforts' standard.
distractor_analysis.C: Supervisory failure occurs through lax oversight of subordinates/delegates, even without co-authoring the false report.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Assess supervisory adequacy, delegation, enforcement, and escalation duties under Standard IV(C)
question: Promoted to Director of Portfolio Management at a fast-growing family office, Nadia Al-Khoury, CFA, discovers the firm has no written compliance manual, no personal trading pre-clearance, and no independent trade review. Al-Khoury submits a detailed compliance budget to the managing partner, who flatly rejects it as 'unnecessary red tape.' Under Standard IV(C), what is Al-Khoury's most appropriate course of action?

options.A: Accept the supervisory role anyway and try to watch employees informally without written policies.
options.B: Wait one full calendar year before raising the compliance budget again.
options.C: Decline in writing to accept supervisory responsibility until the firm adopts reasonable compliance procedures.

explanation: Under Standard IV(C) (Responsibilities of Supervisors), if an employer refuses to establish an adequate compliance system despite the member's recommendations, the member must NOT accept supervisory responsibility over an inadequate system—she must formally decline supervisory responsibility in writing until reasonable procedures are adopted and enforced.

distractor_analysis.A: Informal oversight without an adequate compliance framework leaves the supervisor in ongoing violation of Standard IV(C).
distractor_analysis.B: Delaying a full year while supervising an unmonitored department violates supervisory duties.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Assess supervisory adequacy, delegation, enforcement, and escalation duties under Standard IV(C)
question: Compliance software alerts Chief Investment Officer Victor Ramirez, CFA, that a portfolio manager may have engaged in biased trade allocations favoring a personal friend's trust account over the past quarter. Ramirez immediately suspends the PM's manual allocation permissions, requires dual compliance sign-off on every block trade the PM executes, and launches an independent audit of all historical allocations. Ramirez's response is:

options.A: A violation of Standard IV(C), because he should have terminated the PM on the spot prior to investigating.
options.B: Compliant with Standard IV(C), because he initiated an immediate investigation while placing appropriate interim operational limits on the employee.
options.C: A violation of Standard III(B), because dual sign-off slows trade execution for clients.

explanation: Under Standard IV(C) (Responsibilities of Supervisors), when suspected misconduct is detected, the appropriate supervisory response is to promptly initiate a thorough investigation AND place appropriate interim limitations (such as heightened supervision, dual sign-off, or trading restrictions) on the employee while the inquiry proceeds. Ramirez handled all required steps cleanly.

distractor_analysis.A: Standard IV(C) calls for investigation and interim safeguards rather than summary termination before verifying facts.
distractor_analysis.C: Dual compliance review protects clients from biased allocation and does not violate Standard III(B).

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Assess supervisory adequacy, delegation, enforcement, and escalation duties under Standard IV(C)
question: At onboarding, Sterling Advisors hands every employee a 220-page compliance manual purchased from a legal vendor, covering insider trading, personal account blackouts, and fair allocation. However, Chief Compliance Officer Paul Myers, CFA, never conducts training, never collects brokerage statements, and ignores repeated employee exceptions over three years. No regulatory fine has occurred yet. Under Standard IV(C), Myers has:

options.A: Violated Standard IV(C), because possessing written policies without active implementation, monitoring, and enforcement fails supervisory duty.
options.B: Complied with Standard IV(C), because distributing a comprehensive 220-page manual satisfies reasonable supervision.
options.C: Complied with Standard IV(C), because no regulatory fine or client lawsuit has materialized.

explanation: Under Standard IV(C) (Responsibilities of Supervisors), having an adequate compliance system requires BOTH comprehensive written procedures AND active implementation, training, monitoring, and enforcement. A 'paper manual' sitting unread without trade surveillance or enforcement is inadequate and violates Standard IV(C) even before a client loss or regulatory sanction occurs.

distractor_analysis.B: Written rules without monitoring, training, or enforcement do not meet Standard IV(C).
distractor_analysis.C: Supervisory compliance is evaluated by the adequacy and enforcement of controls, not luck in avoiding regulatory penalties.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Assess supervisory adequacy, delegation, enforcement, and escalation duties under Standard IV(C)
question: Quantitative Strategies Head Lisa Sato, CFA, deploys an automated third-party algorithmic portfolio rebalancing platform across 400 client accounts. Sato grants the software full automated execution access without establishing exception alerts, position-limit circuit breakers, or supervisory validation checks of the algorithm's output. An unchecked bug causes 300% daily turnover across accounts. Sato has violated Standard IV(C) because:

options.A: Quantitative strategies may never use automated execution software.
options.B: Software vendors are solely liable under Standard IV(C) for coding defects.
options.C: Supervisory oversight extends to automated systems, algorithms, and third-party tools operating under the supervisor's authority.

explanation: Under Standard IV(C) (Responsibilities of Supervisors), supervisors are responsible for establishing and enforcing controls over all processes, staff, and automated/AI trading tools operating under their authority. Deploying live automated rebalancing without validation tests, turnover limits, and exception monitoring violates supervisory care.

distractor_analysis.A: Automated trading is permissible when paired with proper validation, risk limits, and ongoing supervisory controls.
distractor_analysis.B: External vendor mistakes do not absolve the firm's supervisor of oversight and risk-control duties.

subtopic: Standard V(A): Diligence and Reasonable Basis
module_title: Standard V(A): Diligence and Reasonable Basis
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate research rigor, secondary research reliance, and group dissent under Standard V(A)
question: Portfolio manager Liam Gallagher, CFA, reads a glowing 20-page equity research initiation from a prestigious bulge-bracket investment bank naming a foreign small-cap diagnostics company its 'Top Conviction Buy.' Impressed by the bank's reputation, Gallagher immediately buys a 5% position for client accounts without reviewing the company's financial filings, clinical trial assumptions, or valuation sensitivity. Gallagher has violated:

options.A: Standard III(E) only, because foreign equities carry currency risk.
options.B: Standard V(A) (Diligence and Reasonable Basis), by relying blindly on third-party research without independently verifying its assumptions and soundness.
options.C: No standard, because bulge-bracket institutional reports are presumed to satisfy reasonable basis.

explanation: Under Standard V(A) (Diligence and Reasonable Basis), members may use secondary or third-party research ONLY after exercising independent due diligence to verify the reasonableness, objectivity, methodology, and assumptions underlying that research. Blindly purchasing a 5% client position based solely on another bank's brand prestige without independent review violates Standard V(A).

distractor_analysis.A: Standard III(E) covers client confidentiality, not investment diligence.
distractor_analysis.C: Brand prestige of a sell-side investment bank never excuses a portfolio manager from conducting independent diligence on third-party reports.

subtopic: Standard V(A): Diligence and Reasonable Basis
module_title: Standard V(A): Diligence and Reasonable Basis
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate research rigor, secondary research reliance, and group dissent under Standard V(A)
question: Quant manager Elena Petrova, CFA, purchases a subscription to a commercial vendor's proprietary machine-learning stock-selection model whose marketing brochure highlights a 12-year backtested Sharpe ratio of 2.9. Because the vendor treats the neural-network architecture as a trade secret, Petrova cannot inspect feature weights; she deploys live client capital immediately without running out-of-sample stress tests, turnover sensitivity checks, or regime-shift simulations. Petrova has violated Standard V(A) primarily because:

options.A: She failed to test and validate the quantitative model's robustness, assumptions, and overfitting risks before deploying client capital.
options.B: Machine-learning quantitative models are categorically banned under the Code and Standards.
options.C: Sharpe ratios above 2.0 require prior written approval from CFA Institute.

explanation: Under Standard V(A) (Diligence and Reasonable Basis), when using external quantitative or AI/ML models, members must understand the model's parameters, assumptions, and limitations, and independently verify robustness—such as testing out-of-sample performance, transaction-cost drag, and stress scenarios—before relying on it for live client recommendations or trades.

distractor_analysis.B: Quantitative and ML models are widely permitted once properly vetted and stress-tested.
distractor_analysis.C: CFA Institute does not pre-approve quantitative models or Sharpe thresholds.

subtopic: Standard V(A): Diligence and Reasonable Basis
module_title: Standard V(A): Diligence and Reasonable Basis
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate research rigor, secondary research reliance, and group dissent under Standard V(A)
question: Analyst Maya Patel, CFA, serves on Horizon Capital's five-member European Equity Committee. Following weeks of thorough financial modeling, channel checks, and scenario analysis, four members vote to upgrade a German automaker to 'Buy.' Patel respectfully disagrees because she places a higher probability on near-term EV battery cost inflation, though she confirms the majority's valuation model is rigorously documented and analytically sound. Patel allows her name to remain on the committee's published 'Buy' report. Patel has:

options.A: Violated Standard V(A), because a dissenting committee member must always remove her name from every report with which she disagrees.
options.B: Violated Standard I(B), because staying on the report shows lack of personal conviction.
options.C: Complied with Standard V(A), because a member need not dissociate from a group consensus report provided the consensus opinion has a reasonable and adequate basis.

explanation: Under Standard V(A) (Diligence and Reasonable Basis), when participating in group research or an investment committee, a member who reaches a different investment conclusion does NOT have to dissociate from the group report so long as the group report itself has a reasonable and adequate basis and reflects diligent, independent analysis. Dissociation is required only if the consensus lacks a reasonable basis or is unethical.

distractor_analysis.A: Mandatory dissociation applies only when a group report lacks a reasonable and adequate basis, not over legitimate analytical disagreement.
distractor_analysis.B: Allowing a well-supported consensus report to go forward with one's team name does not sacrifice objectivity.

subtopic: Standard V(A): Diligence and Reasonable Basis
module_title: Standard V(A): Diligence and Reasonable Basis
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate research rigor, secondary research reliance, and group dissent under Standard V(A)
question: Pension consultant Derek Shaw, CFA, recommends allocating 12% of a municipal pension fund to Crescent Macro, a three-year-old offshore hedge fund. Shaw bases his recommendation solely on Crescent's impressive 18% net annual return summary sheet and a 45-minute lunch meeting with Crescent's charismatic founder, never requesting audited financial statements, prime-broker custody confirmations, or operational risk-control reviews. Shaw's recommendation violates Standard V(A) because:

options.A: Three-year-old hedge funds are ineligible for institutional pension portfolios.
options.B: Selecting an external manager requires comprehensive operational and investment due diligence beyond headline historical returns.
options.C: Meeting a fund manager over lunch violates Standard I(B) hospitality limits.

explanation: Under Standard V(A) (Diligence and Reasonable Basis), recommending a third-party sub-advisor or hedge fund requires thorough investment AND operational due diligence—verifying audited financials, independent custody, valuation policies, risk controls, and consistency of process—not relying superficially on unaudited return tables and an informal lunch.

distractor_analysis.A: Younger funds are not categorically barred if rigorous investment/operational diligence supports suitability and mandate fit.
distractor_analysis.C: A routine 45-minute business lunch is not the core issue; superficial manager selection lacking audited verification breaches V(A).

subtopic: Standard V(A): Diligence and Reasonable Basis
module_title: Standard V(A): Diligence and Reasonable Basis
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate research rigor, secondary research reliance, and group dissent under Standard V(A)
question: Before incorporating macroeconomic GDP and inflation projections from an external independent forecasting consultancy into her fixed-income duration models, analyst Mei Zhou, CFA, audits the consultancy's 10-year forecast error history, checks its econometric assumptions, verifies it receives no funding from bond issuers, and documents how its inputs align with her internal bond valuation framework. Under Standard V(A), Zhou's reliance on the external forecast is:

options.A: Compliant, because she exercised reasonable diligence to validate the third-party provider's methodology, historical accuracy, and objectivity.
options.B: A violation, because members must build every macroeconomic forecast completely in-house without external data.
options.C: A violation, unless the external consultancy employs only CFA charterholders.

explanation: Under Standard V(A) (Diligence and Reasonable Basis), members may rely on third-party research (macro forecasts, credit ratings, sector studies) once they conduct independent due diligence verifying the provider's methodology, assumptions, historical rigor, and freedom from conflicts of interest. Zhou's documented review satisfies Standard V(A) cleanly.

distractor_analysis.B: Standard V(A) explicitly allows using vetted secondary and third-party research rather than forcing redundant creation of all inputs from scratch.
distractor_analysis.C: Third-party research providers need not employ CFA charterholders for their validated work to be relied upon.

subtopic: Standard V(A): Diligence and Reasonable Basis
module_title: Standard V(A): Diligence and Reasonable Basis
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate research rigor, secondary research reliance, and group dissent under Standard V(A)
question: Retail utilities analyst Victor Santos, CFA, updates a 'Buy' recommendation on Regional Grid Corp after skimming the headline quarterly EPS press release. Santos skips reading the Form 10-Q debt footnotes, thereby overlooking a newly triggered covenant acceleration clause requiring 900 million USD in off-balance-sheet joint-venture debt to be refinanced within four months at punitive rates. Two weeks later, the company halts dividends and the stock plunges 38%. Santos has violated Standard V(A) because:

options.A: Utilities analysts are prohibited from relying on quarterly EPS announcements.
options.B: Standard V(A) forbids issuing 'Buy' ratings on leveraged infrastructure companies.
options.C: He failed to exercise thoroughness and diligence by omitting critical footnote review needed to establish a reasonable and adequate basis.

explanation: Under Standard V(A) (Diligence and Reasonable Basis), members must exercise diligence, independence, and thoroughness in analyzing investments. Skimming headline EPS without examining balance-sheet footnotes—missing an imminent 900 million USD debt acceleration risk—leaves the recommendation without a reasonable and adequate basis.

distractor_analysis.A: Press releases may be reviewed alongside primary filings, but never as a substitute for thorough footnote analysis.
distractor_analysis.B: Leveraged utilities can receive Buy ratings when thorough credit and valuation diligence supports the recommendation.

subtopic: Standard V(B): Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
module_title: Standard V(B): Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Apply disclosure rules for investment process changes, risks, and fact-versus-opinion separation under Standard V(B)
question: In a client equity research report on MedTech Innovations, analyst Sarah Lindqvist, CFA, writes: 'MedTech generated 3.10 USD in diluted EPS last fiscal year, and the company will earn 4.65 USD per share next year while expanding operating margins by 340 basis points as its surgical robot captures 28% market share.' Which Standard V(B) requirement has Lindqvist most clearly violated?

options.A: Distinguishing clearly between historical facts and forward-looking opinions or estimates.
options.B: Disclosing her firm's soft-dollar trading policy in every company report.
options.C: Retaining workpapers for at least seven years.

explanation: Under Standard V(B) (Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients), members must clearly distinguish between verifiable historical facts and opinions, projections, or expectations. Presenting next year's projected 4.65 USD EPS, 340 bps margin expansion, and 28% market share as definitive assertions ('will earn') blurred with actual prior-year EPS violates Standard V(B).

distractor_analysis.B: Soft-dollar disclosures fall primarily under Standard III(A) and Standard VI(A), not Standard V(B) report phrasing.
distractor_analysis.C: Record retention is governed by Standard V(C) rather than distinguishing facts from opinions in Standard V(B).

subtopic: Standard V(B): Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
module_title: Standard V(B): Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Apply disclosure rules for investment process changes, risks, and fact-versus-opinion separation under Standard V(B)
question: For nine years, Pioneer Value Partners marketed its flagship fund to clients as 'strictly long-only, unleveraged, bottom-up fundamental value investing.' Seeking to smooth returns during a growth-led rally, lead manager Daniel Cho, CFA, begins borrowing 30% on margin and selling short-dated earnings-straddle options on momentum stocks—without informing existing clients or updating offering communications. Cho's conduct violates Standard V(B) primarily because he failed to:

options.A: Avoid using any options or margin leverage across all mutual funds.
options.B: Promptly disclose material changes in the basic format, general principles, and risks of the investment process.
options.C: Obtain independent GIPS verification prior to adding an options overlay.

explanation: Under Standard V(B) (Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients), members must disclose the basic format and general principles of their investment process and PROMPTLY disclose any changes that might materially affect those processes, along with significant associated risks. Quietly adding 30% margin leverage and short-term earnings option straddles to an unleveraged value process breaches Standard V(B) (and III(C)).

distractor_analysis.A: Options and leverage are permissible when permitted by the mandate and properly disclosed with risks.
distractor_analysis.C: GIPS verification is voluntary and unrelated to timely process-change disclosures under Standard V(B).

subtopic: Standard V(B): Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
module_title: Standard V(B): Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Apply disclosure rules for investment process changes, risks, and fact-versus-opinion separation under Standard V(B)
question: Private bank advisor Marcus Bell, CFA, distributes a sleek two-page marketing flyer promoting a five-year structured note linked to European bank stocks. The headline boldly promises '11.5% Annual Target Coupon with Principal Buffer Features.' Nowhere in the flyer does Bell mention that the note carries 100% unsecured single-issuer credit risk of the underwriting bank, includes an issuer call feature capping upside, and has no liquid secondary market. Burying those details in a separate 140-page prospectus provided only at closing violates Standard V(B) because:

options.A: Structured notes may never be advertised in two-page flyers.
options.B: Target coupons above 10% automatically breach Standard I(C).
options.C: Communications must disclose significant limitations and risks associated with the investment process and product rather than omitting material downsides.

explanation: Under Standard V(B) (Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients), members must disclose significant limitations and risks associated with recommended investments and include all important analytical factors. Highlighting an 11.5% coupon in promotional summaries while omitting single-issuer credit risk, call risk, and illiquidity misleads clients under Standard V(B).

distractor_analysis.A: Summary flyers are permissible when key risks and limitations are accurately presented alongside return features.
distractor_analysis.B: Yield level alone does not establish a violation if clearly labeled as conditional and paired with prominent risk disclosures.

subtopic: Standard V(B): Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
module_title: Standard V(B): Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Apply disclosure rules for investment process changes, risks, and fact-versus-opinion separation under Standard V(B)
question: Following an exhaustive 35-page DCF and credit valuation of Horizon Logistics, equity analyst Priya Desai, CFA, emails clients a concise one-page executive summary. The summary clearly distinguishes historical revenues from estimated future cash flows, states the main valuation assumptions (WACC and terminal growth), highlights key downside risks (freight recession and refinancing spread sensitivity), and informs recipients that the complete 35-page research report and sensitivity tables are available on the client portal. Under Standard V(B), Desai's summary note is:

options.A: Compliant, because concise capsule summaries may omit granular modeling details if key factors, risks, and fact-opinion distinctions are preserved and full documentation is accessible.
options.B: A violation, because every client email must reproduce 100% of all spreadsheet sensitivity tables.
options.C: A violation, because DCF valuation assumptions may not be summarized in less than five pages.

explanation: Under Standard V(B) (Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients), capsule summaries or brief electronic updates comply with Standard V(B) provided the member uses reasonable judgment to include key factors, preserves the distinction between fact and opinion, discloses material risks/limitations, and notifies clients how to access the full detailed report.

distractor_analysis.B: Reproducing entire 35-page appendices in every email is unnecessary when full reports are transparently made available.
distractor_analysis.C: Standard V(B) imposes no minimum page count; clarity, balance, and inclusion of important factors govern.

subtopic: Standard V(B): Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
module_title: Standard V(B): Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Apply disclosure rules for investment process changes, risks, and fact-versus-opinion separation under Standard V(B)
question: During a pitch for a distressed middle-market direct lending fund, portfolio manager Trevor Vance, CFA, emphasizes its low historical reported return volatility (2.4% annualized) without explaining that the underlying loans do not trade on exchanges, are valued only quarterly via internal appraisal models (creating artificial price smoothing), and impose a two-year redemption gate. Vance has most directly violated Standard V(B) by failing to disclose:

options.A: Exact tax identification numbers of underlying corporate borrowers.
