options.B: Significant valuation methodology limitations, stale-pricing effects, and illiquidity constraints.
options.C: Daily mark-to-market bid-ask spreads on US Treasury futures.

explanation: Under Standard V(B) (Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients), members must communicate significant limitations and risks of their investment process and valuation methodology. Presenting appraisal-smoothed 2.4% volatility as low risk while omitting illiquidity, two-year gates, and model-based quarterly pricing conceals crucial limitations from investors.

distractor_analysis.A: Borrower tax IDs are irrelevant and potentially confidential; the breach concerns hiding appraisal-smoothing and gate risks.
distractor_analysis.C: Treasury futures spreads are unrelated to disclosing direct-lending valuation and liquidity constraints.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Determine record-retention responsibilities, employer ownership, and archival timeframes under Standard V(C)
question: Before leaving Apex Securities to join Rival Capital, healthcare analyst Claire Novak, CFA, copies onto a personal hard drive 150 Excel financial models, clinical interview transcripts, and site-visit notebooks that she personally compiled during her five years at Apex. When challenged by Apex compliance, Novak claims she is required to keep those files to fulfill Standard V(C) (Record Retention) at her new employer. Novak's argument is:

options.A: Correct, because Standard V(C) obligates individual analysts to carry personal copies of historical research wherever they work.
options.B: Correct with respect to her personal handwritten site-visit notebooks, though not Excel files.
options.C: Incorrect, because supporting research records created during employment belong to the employer, and departing analysts must re-create support from public sources at their new firm.

explanation: Under Standard V(C) (Record Retention) and Standard IV(A) (Loyalty), investment research records, models, and notes compiled during employment are the property of the employer (firm), not the individual employee. Departing analysts may not take original or copied firm records without employer permission; to re-issue recommendations at a new firm, they must re-create supporting documentation from public sources.

distractor_analysis.A: Record-retention accountability at Firm A stays with Firm A; individual portability of proprietary firm files is prohibited.
distractor_analysis.B: Handwritten field notes and site-visit workpapers compiled on employer business are also firm property.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Determine record-retention responsibilities, employer ownership, and archival timeframes under Standard V(C)
question: To streamline fast communication with busy entrepreneur clients, wealth advisor Lucas Ortega, CFA, discusses specific stock buy/sell recommendations, risk-tolerance modifications, and execution rationales using an encrypted smartphone messaging application configured to automatically delete all messages after 24 hours. Neither Ortega nor his firm archives those chats. Ortega's practice violates Standard V(C) because:

options.A: Electronic communications conveying investment recommendations, rationales, and client instructions must be captured and retained as firm records.
options.B: Smartphone encryption violates Standard III(E) confidentiality.
options.C: Standard V(C) bans discussing investments with clients via any digital channel.

explanation: Under Standard V(C) (Record Retention), members must develop and maintain appropriate records—across both physical and electronic media—supporting investment analyses, recommendations, actions, and client communications. Using auto-deleting ephemeral messaging apps for client investment advice prevents archival verification and directly violates Standard V(C).

distractor_analysis.B: Encryption helps confidentiality under III(E); the violation is automatic deletion destroying required audit trails under V(C).
distractor_analysis.C: Digital channels (email, archived portals, logged messaging) are fully compliant once properly archived.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Determine record-retention responsibilities, employer ownership, and archival timeframes under Standard V(C)
question: Boutique investment advisor Harborview Management operates in a local jurisdiction whose statutory securities rules require retaining client trade tickets and research files for only two years. To save cloud storage expenses, Harborview's operations policy permanently purges all research memos, model backups, and client recommendation logs at the 24-month mark. Absent stricter local legal rules, what minimum retention horizon does CFA Institute recommend under Standard V(C)?

options.A: Three years from the date of initial security purchase.
options.B: At least seven years.
options.C: Indefinitely in physical paper binders only.

explanation: Under the recommended procedures for Standard V(C) (Record Retention), in the absence of stricter local regulatory requirements, CFA Institute recommends maintaining supporting investment records—whether in hard copy or electronic format—for at least seven years.

distractor_analysis.A: Three years falls short of CFA Institute's seven-year recommended benchmark.
distractor_analysis.C: Electronic archival is expressly acceptable (and often preferred), and the baseline recommended horizon is seven years rather than mandatory indefinite paper storage.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Determine record-retention responsibilities, employer ownership, and archival timeframes under Standard V(C)
question: After resigning honorably from Sterling Asset Management without taking any files, notes, or valuation spreadsheets, industrial analyst Devon Patel, CFA, joins Cascade Investments. Before publishing a new 'Buy' initiation on Global Freight Corp—a company Patel previously covered at Sterling—Patel downloads public SEC 10-K filings, earnings call transcripts, and industry freight volume data at Cascade, builds a fresh valuation model from scratch, and archives all supporting files in Cascade's research repository. Under Standard V(C), Patel has:

options.A: Violated Standard V(C) by covering the same company he analyzed at his previous firm.
options.B: Violated Standard IV(A) by remembering Global Freight Corp's ticker symbol.
options.C: Complied fully with Standard V(C) by re-creating supporting research records from public sources for his new employer's archives.

explanation: Under Standard V(C) (Record Retention) and Standard IV(A) (Loyalty), when an analyst moves to a new firm without taking prior firm files and wishes to cover a previously analyzed issuer, the proper compliant path is to rebuild the analysis and supporting documentation completely from public sources and save those newly created records in the new employer's repository.

distractor_analysis.A: Covering the same industry or issuer at a new firm is entirely permissible using fresh public research.
distractor_analysis.B: General industry expertise and public company names are not confidential employer property.

subtopic: Standard VI(A): Avoid or Disclose Conflicts
module_title: Standard VI(A): Avoid or Disclose Conflicts
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate prominence, plain-language clarity, and scope of conflict disclosures under Standard VI(A)
question: Investment bank and brokerage firm Horizon Securities acts as co-manager for a secondary equity offering of BioPulse Ltd and owns 400,000 BioPulse stock warrants received as underwriting compensation. When publishing an institutional 'Outperform' report on BioPulse, Horizon places its disclosure of the underwriting fee and warrant holdings in 8-point italic legal text buried inside Note 19 on page 29 of an attached general compliance appendix. Under Standard VI(A), this disclosure is:

options.A: Insufficient, because disclosures of material conflicts must be prominent, delivered in plain language, and communicate relevant information effectively.
options.B: Compliant, because any written mention anywhere inside the distributed PDF fulfills Standard VI(A).
options.C: Insufficient solely because warrants must be sold before any research coverage begins.

explanation: Under Standard VI(A) (Avoid or Disclose Conflicts), disclosure is effective only when it is PROMINENT, stated in plain language, and communicates the nature of the conflict clearly to readers (typically on the front page or dedicated prominent disclosure section of a research report). Burying material underwriting fees and warrant ownership in fine-print boilerplate on page 29 fails Standard VI(A).

distractor_analysis.B: Obscuring conflicts in dense back-page boilerplate violates the prominence and effective communication standard.
distractor_analysis.C: Holding warrants does not automatically prohibit coverage if the conflict is managed properly and prominently disclosed.

subtopic: Standard VI(A): Avoid or Disclose Conflicts
module_title: Standard VI(A): Avoid or Disclose Conflicts
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate prominence, plain-language clarity, and scope of conflict disclosures under Standard VI(A)
question: Biotech analyst Martin Chen, CFA, initiates coverage on GeneTherapeutics Inc. with a strong 'Buy' recommendation. Chen's spouse owns 150,000 USD in vested GeneTherapeutics stock options earned during prior employment there. Chen discloses his spouse's option holdings in writing to his Research Director and Compliance Department, who clear him to publish the report, yet the published client report contains zero mention of the spousal option stake. Chen has violated Standard VI(A) because:

options.A: Spousal holdings never require disclosure if the analyst holds no shares personally.
options.B: Material beneficial ownership conflicts must be disclosed not only to the employer, but also prominently to clients and prospective clients reading the recommendation.
options.C: Compliance pre-clearance automatically transfers all disclosure liability to the Research Director.

explanation: Under Standard VI(A) (Avoid or Disclose Conflicts), members must disclose all matters that could reasonably impair independence and objectivity to ALL affected parties—meaning BOTH the employer AND clients/prospective clients. Disclosing a spouse's 150,000 USD vested option stake internally to Compliance without disclosing it in the published client report leaves clients uninformed of the conflict.

distractor_analysis.A: Spousal financial holdings represent indirect beneficial/household interests that can clearly impair objectivity.
distractor_analysis.C: Internal clearance by Compliance does not excuse omitting mandatory client-facing conflict disclosures.

subtopic: Standard VI(A): Avoid or Disclose Conflicts
module_title: Standard VI(A): Avoid or Disclose Conflicts
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate prominence, plain-language clarity, and scope of conflict disclosures under Standard VI(A)
question: Senior equity portfolio manager Nora Takahashi, CFA, accepts an invitation to serve as an unpaid independent member of the Board of Directors of Solaris Medical Corp, a publicly traded firm whose shares fall within the investable universe of her clients' growth portfolios. Takahashi holds no Solaris shares personally. To comply with Standard VI(A), Takahashi must:

options.A: Skip disclosure entirely because her directorship is unpaid.
options.B: Disclose the directorship only to Solaris Medical's corporate secretary.
options.C: Disclose the board membership prominently to both her employer and her clients/prospective clients, and implement controls around potential conflicts and material nonpublic information.

explanation: Under Standard VI(A) (Avoid or Disclose Conflicts), serving on a public company's board—even unpaid—creates significant conflicts of interest between fiduciary duties to corporate shareholders and duties to investment clients (plus exposure to MNPI under Standard II(A)). Takahashi must disclose the board service to BOTH her employer and clients/prospective clients, and follow firm conflict/restriction protocols.

distractor_analysis.A: Lack of director compensation does not eliminate conflicting fiduciary loyalties and reputational incentives.
distractor_analysis.B: Her employer and advisory clients are the affected investment stakeholders requiring full conflict disclosure.

subtopic: Standard VI(A): Avoid or Disclose Conflicts
module_title: Standard VI(A): Avoid or Disclose Conflicts
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate prominence, plain-language clarity, and scope of conflict disclosures under Standard VI(A)
question: Wealth advisor Kevin Morales, CFA, works at a dual-registered firm offering both low-cost third-party ETFs and proprietary actively managed multi-asset funds. Under the firm's payout schedule, Morales receives a 1.50% upfront sales credit when placing clients into proprietary funds versus 0.15% on third-party ETFs. Morales routinely recommends the proprietary funds to new clients without disclosing this tenfold payout differential. Morales has violated Standard VI(A) by failing to:

options.A: Disclose an incentive compensation structure that could reasonably bias his product recommendations.
options.B: Charge identical 1.50% fees across all third-party ETFs.
options.C: Avoid all proprietary products in retail wealth accounts.

explanation: Under Standard VI(A) (Avoid or Disclose Conflicts), compensation differentials—such as earning 10 times higher sales credits on proprietary products than external ETFs—create an obvious financial incentive that can impair objectivity. Failing to disclose this conflict prominently in plain language to clients and prospects violates Standard VI(A).

distractor_analysis.B: Uniformity of fees is not required, whereas transparent upfront disclosure of conflicting compensation incentives is mandatory.
distractor_analysis.C: Proprietary funds may be offered when suitable and when compensation conflicts are prominently disclosed.

subtopic: Standard VI(A): Avoid or Disclose Conflicts
module_title: Standard VI(A): Avoid or Disclose Conflicts
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate prominence, plain-language clarity, and scope of conflict disclosures under Standard VI(A)
question: Regional bank analyst Rachel Foster, CFA, covers Heartland Bancorp. Heartland recently hired Foster's brother as its Chief Financial Officer. Confident in her analytical integrity and knowing she will maintain strict objectivity, Foster declines to notify her research supervisor or add a disclosure note to her upcoming Heartland earnings update. Under Standard VI(A), Foster has:

options.A: Complied, because personal integrity prevents actual bias in her financial models.
options.B: Violated Standard VI(A), because a close family member holding a senior executive post at a covered company creates a material conflict requiring disclosure (or reassignment).
options.C: Complied, provided she never discusses quarterly earnings with her brother at family gatherings.

explanation: Under Standard VI(A) (Avoid or Disclose Conflicts), disclosure depends on whether a matter could REASONABLY BE EXPECTED to impair objectivity or create the appearance of conflict in the eyes of clients and employer—not the analyst's subjective confidence in her own willpower. Having a sibling serve as CFO of a covered bank must be disclosed to employer and clients (or coverage reassigned).

distractor_analysis.A: Subjective confidence in one's objectivity never waives Standard VI(A) disclosure obligations.
distractor_analysis.C: Avoiding insider conversations addresses Standard II(A), but does not eliminate the reportable conflict under Standard VI(A).

subtopic: Standard VI(A): Avoid or Disclose Conflicts
module_title: Standard VI(A): Avoid or Disclose Conflicts
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate prominence, plain-language clarity, and scope of conflict disclosures under Standard VI(A)
question: Quantitative portfolio manager Oliver Grant, CFA, is employed full time managing global macro hedge funds at Titan Capital. Outside work, Grant is invited to join his university's volunteer Endowment Investment Committee, which actively allocates capital across competing global macro hedge funds and occasionally co-invests in the same sovereign bond auctions Titan targets. To adhere to Standard VI(A), Grant must:

options.A: Accept quietly without notifying Titan Capital because the university role is unpaid.
options.B: Notify only the university endowment board about his job at Titan Capital.
options.C: Disclose the outside committee role and potential strategy/allocation overlap to his employer before accepting.

explanation: Under Standard VI(A) (Avoid or Disclose Conflicts), members must disclose any outside duties, board seats, or investment committee memberships that could interfere with their duties to their employer or create competing/conflicting market allocations. Even though unpaid, participating in macro manager selection and sovereign co-investments directly intersects with Titan Capital's business and requires prior disclosure to the employer.

distractor_analysis.A: Unpaid status does not prevent competitive or time/information conflicts with the employer.
distractor_analysis.B: Standard VI(A) explicitly requires disclosing conflicts affecting employer duties to the employer.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Apply transaction priority rules among clients, employers, and beneficial ownership accounts under Standard VI(B)
question: At 9:00 AM, Apex Investment Partners releases a firm-wide research upgrade on OmniCorp from 'Hold' to 'Buy.' Portfolio manager Sophia Rossi, CFA, executes buy orders across all suitable client accounts at 9:35 AM. After all client orders are completely filled, Apex's proprietary trading desk executes its OmniCorp purchase at 10:30 AM. Following the firm's mandatory 48-hour employee trading blackout window, Rossi receives compliance pre-clearance and buys 200 shares for her personal IRA two days later. Under Standard VI(B), Rossi's trade sequence is:

options.A: Compliant, because transactions followed the required priority order: clients first, employer second, and personal beneficial accounts last.
options.B: A violation, because portfolio managers may never buy securities held in client accounts.
options.C: A violation, because the employer's proprietary desk must trade before client accounts.

explanation: Under Standard VI(B) (Priority of Transactions), investment transactions for clients and employers must have priority over transactions in which a member or candidate is the beneficial owner. The strict hierarchy is: (1) Clients first, (2) Employer second, and (3) Personal/beneficial accounts last after required blackout/pre-clearance periods. Rossi followed every requirement.

distractor_analysis.B: Personal ownership of covered securities is permissible once client/employer priority, blackout rules, pre-clearance, and VI(A) disclosures are observed.
distractor_analysis.C: Client transactions always take priority over the employer's proprietary trading desk.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Apply transaction priority rules among clients, employers, and beneficial ownership accounts under Standard VI(B)
question: Small-cap portfolio manager Nathan Patel, CFA, submits orders for 15,000 shares of a hot software IPO across 12 eligible discretionary client accounts, which receive only a 60% partial fill (9,000 shares). Simultaneously, Patel places an order for 500 shares in his wife's IRA—an account in which he holds no trading title on paper—and receives a full 500-share allotment because his wife's account is maintained as an individual brokerage relationship at the firm. Patel has violated Standard VI(B) because:

options.A: Spouses of portfolio managers are prohibited from opening IRAs.
options.B: Partial fills require canceling all client IPO allocations.
options.C: A spouse's account represents a beneficial ownership interest that must stand behind unsatisfied client orders.

explanation: Under Standard VI(B) (Priority of Transactions), 'beneficial owner' encompasses any account in which a member has a direct or indirect pecuniary interest or shares household financial benefit—explicitly including a spouse's or dependent child's account. Allocating oversubscribed IPO shares to a spouse's IRA while client orders remain partially unfilled directly violates Standard VI(B).

distractor_analysis.A: Spouses may maintain IRAs, but those accounts are treated as member-beneficial accounts under personal trading and IPO priority rules.
distractor_analysis.B: Client partial fills are allocated pro rata under III(B); they are not canceled because of personal/spousal conflicts.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Apply transaction priority rules among clients, employers, and beneficial ownership accounts under Standard VI(B)
question: At 10:10 AM, equity trader Julian Brooks, CFA, receives an institutional pension client's order to purchase 1.8 million shares of an illiquid mid-cap industrial stock over the day. Knowing the massive buy flow will drive the share price higher, Brooks buys 4,000 shares in his personal brokerage account at 10:15 AM before releasing the pension's initial block slice to the market at 10:30 AM. Brooks's conduct most directly violates:

options.A: Standard III(C) only, because mid-cap stocks are illiquid.
options.B: Standard VI(B) (Priority of Transactions), by front-running a pending client order for personal profit.
options.C: Standard VII(A), because trading ahead of clients undermines CFA exam security.

explanation: Front-running a pending client order by executing a personal trade ahead of client execution violates Standard VI(B) (Priority of Transactions)—as well as Standard III(A) (Loyalty) and Standard II(B) (Market Manipulation) if used to distort prices. Client transactions must always precede personal transactions.

distractor_analysis.A: The core violation is personal front-running of a client order, not suitability of mid-cap exposure.
distractor_analysis.C: Standard VII(A) applies to CFA Program exam conduct and member integrity, not securities front-running.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Apply transaction priority rules among clients, employers, and beneficial ownership accounts under Standard VI(B)
question: Prior to becoming Head of Consumer Research at Meridian Capital, Elena Rostova, CFA, establishes an irrevocable blind trust managed entirely by an independent third-party bank trustee. Under the trust instrument, Rostova has zero investment discretion, receives no advance trade notifications, and cannot direct or influence security selection. Without Rostova's knowledge, the independent trustee purchases shares in a beverage stock covered by Rostova two days before she upgrades the stock. Under Standard VI(B) recommended compliance procedures, Rostova has:

options.A: Not violated Standard VI(B), because genuine blind trusts over which the member exercises zero influence or knowledge are normally exempt from pre-clearance and blackout restrictions.
options.B: Violated Standard VI(B), because a blind trust is treated identically to an active personal brokerage account.
options.C: Violated Standard VI(B), unless she immediately forces the independent trustee to liquidate the beverage shares at a loss.

explanation: Recommended procedures for Standard VI(B) (Priority of Transactions) distinguish accounts where the member exercises investment influence from genuine blind trusts or fully independent discretionary accounts/diversified mutual funds where the member has zero knowledge, communication, or control over individual security timing. Because Rostova exercised no knowledge or influence, no Standard VI(B) violation occurred.

distractor_analysis.B: True blind trusts are recognized exemptions under personal trading pre-clearance and blackout frameworks.
distractor_analysis.C: Forcing the independent trustee to sell would actually breach the blind trust's non-interference boundary.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Apply transaction priority rules among clients, employers, and beneficial ownership accounts under Standard VI(B)
question: Meridian Investment Bank's proprietary trading desk places an order for 50,000 shares of a newly listed robotics IPO, but receives only 20,000 shares (all client demand having already been fully satisfied). Meanwhile, proprietary analyst Trevor Kim, CFA, who received no client allocations, purchases 1,000 shares of the same robotics IPO in his personal brokerage account during the initial offering allocation. Under Standard VI(B), Kim's purchase:

options.A: Complied, because all external client orders were completely satisfied.
options.B: Complied, because analysts are unrelated to the firm's proprietary desk.
options.C: Violated Standard VI(B), because transactions for the employer must also take priority over transactions in accounts where a member is beneficial owner.

explanation: Standard VI(B) (Priority of Transactions) requires that investment transactions for BOTH clients AND employers have priority over personal transactions in which the member is a beneficial owner. Even after external client orders are filled, an employee cannot participate in a scarce IPO allocation ahead of or to the detriment of an unfilled employer proprietary order.

distractor_analysis.A: Client priority is only the first tier; the employer's transaction priority still supersedes employee personal accounts.
distractor_analysis.B: Standard VI(B) binds all members and candidates regarding their employer's orders regardless of department.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Assess timing, content, and recipient rules for referral fee disclosures under Standard VI(C)
question: Independent wealth advisor Clara Vance, CFA, signs a referral agreement paying an external Certified Public Accountant (CPA) 20% of first-year advisory fees for every wealthy tax client the CPA refers to Vance's firm. Vance discloses this payment arrangement in writing to her firm's Chief Compliance Officer, but neither Vance nor the CPA mentions the 20% fee split to referred prospective clients prior to signing investment management agreements. Vance has violated Standard VI(C) because:

options.A: Paying cash referral fees to CPAs is banned outright under the Code and Standards.
options.B: Referral fees paid to—not merely received from—outside parties must be disclosed to clients and prospective clients before entering into an agreement.
options.C: Only referral fees exceeding 50% of annual advisory fees require prospect disclosure.

explanation: Under Standard VI(C) (Referral Fees), members must disclose to their employer, clients, and prospective clients any compensation, consideration, or benefit RECEIVED FROM OR PAID TO others for the recommendation of products or services. Disclosure to prospects must occur BEFORE entering into any formal service agreement so clients can evaluate the referrer's bias.

distractor_analysis.A: Referral fees are permitted when disclosed upfront in plain terms (nature and estimated value/percentage) to employer, clients, and prospects.
distractor_analysis.C: Standard VI(C) applies to any material referral benefit regardless of percentage threshold.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Assess timing, content, and recipient rules for referral fee disclosures under Standard VI(C)
question: Private client advisor Liam Shaw, CFA, routinely refers high-net-worth clients needing complex trust drafting to an external estate law firm. Rather than paying Shaw cash, the law firm gives Shaw complimentary use of its luxury stadium box suite for client entertainment plus three free hours of personal legal drafting for every client referred. Shaw does not inform his employer or referred clients of these benefits. Shaw's omission violates Standard VI(C) because:

options.A: Standard VI(C) covers any non-cash consideration or benefit, not strictly direct cash commissions.
options.B: Estate law referrals are covered only under Standard I(B) hospitality rules.
options.C: Disclosures apply exclusively when the advisor pays fees out of pocket.

explanation: Standard VI(C) (Referral Fees) applies broadly to 'any compensation, consideration, or benefit received from or paid to others'—explicitly covering non-cash perks, complimentary personal legal services, stadium suites, soft-dollar credits, or reciprocal business arrangements. Failing to disclose these benefits to employer and clients breaches Standard VI(C).

distractor_analysis.B: Quid-pro-quo benefits tied directly to client referrals trigger Standard VI(C) referral disclosures in addition to conflict rules.
distractor_analysis.C: Standard VI(C) covers benefits both received from and paid to external parties.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Assess timing, content, and recipient rules for referral fee disclosures under Standard VI(C)
question: Boutique asset manager Apex Wealth receives a client referral from an outside insurance broker, to whom Apex pays an ongoing 25-basis-point annual AUM trail. Ten days AFTER the new client signs Apex's advisory contract and transfers 2 million USD, Apex mails a welcome packet containing a footnote stating: 'Apex may occasionally pay referral compensation to third parties.' Which two flaws place Apex advisor Thomas Grant, CFA, in violation of Standard VI(C)?

options.A: Paying an ongoing AUM trail instead of a flat fee, and using postal mail.
options.B: Working with insurance brokers, and accepting transfers above 1 million USD.
options.C: Disclosing after contract execution instead of beforehand, and omitting the nature and estimated dollar value or formula of the fee.

explanation: Under Standard VI(C) (Referral Fees), disclosure must occur BEFORE entering into a formal agreement for services so the prospective client can make an informed decision. Moreover, disclosure must communicate BOTH the nature of the consideration (ongoing 25 bps trail) and its estimated dollar value (here, 5,000 USD annually on 2 million USD)—vague post-contract 'may occasionally pay' footnotes fail both requirements.

distractor_analysis.A: Ongoing AUM trails and postal disclosures are permissible when properly structured, timed upfront, and quantified.
distractor_analysis.B: Referral relationships with insurance brokers and large account sizes are normal and compliant once properly disclosed.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Assess timing, content, and recipient rules for referral fee disclosures under Standard VI(C)
question: Mortgage specialist Priya Nair, CFA, partners with an independent wealth advisor who refers homebuyers seeking jumbo mortgages. Nair pays the external wealth advisor a flat 500 USD referral fee per closed loan. Before accepting any loan application from a referred client, Nair obtains written sign-off from her employer and hands the prospective borrower a standalone one-page plain-English disclosure stating the exact 500 USD flat referral payment and who receives it. Under Standard VI(C), Nair has:

options.A: Violated Standard VI(C), because flat-dollar referral payments are prohibited.
options.B: Complied fully with Standard VI(C) by disclosing the nature and exact amount of the fee to both her employer and prospective clients prior to formal engagement.
options.C: Violated Standard VI(C), because referral disclosures must be hidden inside closing escrow statements.

explanation: Nair satisfied every requirement of Standard VI(C) (Referral Fees): she disclosed the external referral payment to her employer, presented a prominent plain-English disclosure detailing both the nature (flat referral fee) and exact dollar amount (500 USD) to prospective clients BEFORE entering any formal lending agreement.

distractor_analysis.A: Flat-dollar, percentage, and non-cash referral fees are all permissible when transparently disclosed upfront.
distractor_analysis.C: Prominent standalone pre-agreement disclosure is ideal and vastly superior to burying notices in closing documents.

subtopic: Standard VII(A): Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs
module_title: Standard VII(A): Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate exam security, confidential testing rules, and program integrity under Standard VII(A)
question: Hours after completing the CFA Level I exam, registered candidate Ethan Brooks posts in an online study forum: 'What a relief—I completely skipped reviewing GIPS verification rules and two-period binomial option trees during my final week, and luckily neither topic appeared anywhere on today's exam!' Has Brooks violated Standard VII(A)?

options.A: Yes, because disclosing confidential information about which specific curriculum topics were or were not tested compromises exam security.
options.B: No, because he did not quote exact numerical questions or answer choices from the exam.
options.C: No, because exam confidentiality applies only to CFA charterholders rather than Level I candidates.

explanation: Under Standard VII(A) (Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs), candidates and members must not compromise the integrity, validity, or security of CFA exams. Disclosing confidential exam details includes revealing NOT ONLY specific questions, but also which curriculum topics, formulas, or reading areas were or were NOT tested on a particular exam sitting.

distractor_analysis.B: Even confirming which specific subjects were absent from the exam leaks protected exam content structure to subsequent test takers.
distractor_analysis.C: Standard VII(A) explicitly binds all registered CFA Program candidates as well as active members.

subtopic: Standard VII(A): Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs
module_title: Standard VII(A): Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate exam security, confidential testing rules, and program integrity under Standard VII(A)
question: After exiting the testing center for her CFA Level II examination, candidate Maya Alvarez writes on her social media page: 'Just finished Level II! The afternoon item sets were mentally exhausting and I barely managed my pacing on the final session, but I'm glad to be done and celebrating tonight.' Alvarez mentions no specific readings, formulas, or tested subjects. Under Standard VII(A), Alvarez's post is:

options.A: A violation, because candidates are prohibited from publicly mentioning that they sat for a CFA exam.
options.B: A violation, because commenting on exam time pacing breaches testing security.
options.C: Compliant, because expressing general personal feelings about exam difficulty or time pressure without revealing tested or untested content does not compromise exam security.

explanation: Under Standard VII(A) (Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs), candidates are free to share general opinions about how they felt during the exam (difficulty, fatigue, time management) provided they reveal zero specifics regarding what curriculum topics, vignettes, or formulas were or were not tested.

distractor_analysis.A: Candidates are permitted to state they sat for an exam and discuss general non-content impressions.
distractor_analysis.B: Commenting that one felt rushed on pacing reveals nothing about exam questions or topic coverage.

subtopic: Standard VII(A): Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs
module_title: Standard VII(A): Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate exam security, confidential testing rules, and program integrity under Standard VII(A)
question: Having passed all three CFA exam levels, applicant Victor Novak completes his CFA charter application. Lacking six months of qualified investment decision-making work experience, Novak persuades a friendly former boss to sign an inflated job description exaggerating his clerical operations role as 'direct institutional portfolio management.' Novak also omits a minor regulatory fine on his annual Professional Conduct Statement (PCS). Novak has violated:

options.A: Standard IV(B) only, because his former boss assisted him without compensation.
options.B: Standard VII(A) (Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs), by falsifying work-experience credentials and omitting required PCS disclosures.
options.C: Standard III(D), because misstating job duties distorts firm composite performance.

explanation: Under Standard VII(A) (Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs), misconduct extends beyond exam-day cheating to include falsifying or misrepresenting qualified work experience on charter applications, forging supervisor references, or submitting false/incomplete information on the annual Professional Conduct Statement (PCS).

distractor_analysis.A: Standard IV(B) governs outside compensation conflicting with an employer, not falsifying CFA Institute charter applications.
distractor_analysis.C: Standard III(D) applies to investment performance presentations, whereas falsifying CFA credential applications breaches Standard VII(A).

subtopic: Standard VII(A): Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs
module_title: Standard VII(A): Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate exam security, confidential testing rules, and program integrity under Standard VII(A)
question: During the final seconds of the CFA Level I morning session, the proctor announces over the loudspeaker: 'Time is up. Stop writing immediately and set down your pencils and calculators.' Candidate Kevin Ortiz keeps punching numbers into his financial calculator for 15 extra seconds to finish flagging a final multiple-choice answer on screen before the proctor intervenes. Under Standard VII(A), Ortiz has:

options.A: Violated Standard VII(A) by failing to comply with testing rules and proctor instructions, compromising exam fairness and integrity.
options.B: Complied with Standard VII(A), provided his final calculation changed no more than one answer.
options.C: Violated Standard IV(A) only, because candidates owe loyalty to proctors.

explanation: Under Standard VII(A) (Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs), candidates must adhere strictly to all CFA Institute exam policies and proctor instructions—including stopping immediately when time expires and keeping unauthorized devices out of testing rooms. Continuing to work after 'stop' is called compromises exam fairness and violates Standard VII(A).

distractor_analysis.B: Any unauthorized extra work after time expires—even affecting a single question—violates exam rules under Standard VII(A).
distractor_analysis.C: Standard IV(A) covers loyalty to employers, whereas testing room infractions are governed by Standard VII(A).

subtopic: Standard VII(A): Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs
module_title: Standard VII(A): Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Evaluate exam security, confidential testing rules, and program integrity under Standard VII(A)
question: Charterholder Samuel Park, CFA, serves as an unpaid volunteer on a CFA Institute exam-development review panel, signing strict non-disclosure agreements. Six months later, Park launches a commercial CFA exam-prep tutoring company and writes a paid mock-exam booklet containing several lightly disguised vignettes copied closely from confidential draft items he reviewed on the volunteer panel. Park's actions violate:

options.A: Standard III(E) only, because draft exam items are client records.
options.B: Standard VII(B) only, because he used 'CFA' in advertising a tutoring business.
options.C: Standard VII(A) (Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs), by misusing confidential volunteer access to compromise exam integrity.

explanation: Under Standard VII(A) (Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs), CFA Institute volunteers who participate in curriculum or exam development must strictly protect confidential program materials and never leverage non-public exam knowledge for commercial prep products or personal advantage. Replicating draft exam items violates Standard VII(A) (and I(D)/IV(A)).

distractor_analysis.A: Draft exam items are confidential CFA Institute program property under VII(A), not client account data under III(E).
distractor_analysis.B: Simply describing a tutoring service for CFA candidates is permissible if accurate; stealing confidential exam content violates VII(A).

subtopic: Standard VII(B): Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program
module_title: Standard VII(B): Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Identify proper and improper references to CFA candidacy, membership, and the CFA designation under Standard VII(B)
question: Charterholder Rachel Chen, CFA, launches an independent wealth boutique and prints the following tagline on her business cards and website homepage: 'ChenCFA Wealth Advisors — Hire Certified Financial Advisors: Our team of CFAs delivers disciplined portfolio governance.' Which two errors in Chen's tagline violate Standard VII(B)?

options.A: Claiming disciplined portfolio governance, and printing a tagline on a business card.
options.B: Embedding 'CFA' inside a firm name ('ChenCFA') and using 'CFA' as a plural noun ('CFAs').
options.C: Using the word 'team' on a boutique website, and mentioning 'wealth advisors.'

explanation: Under Standard VII(B) (Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program), the 'CFA' designation must NEVER be used as a noun ('a CFA' or 'CFAs')—it must always be used as an adjective ('CFA charterholder') or post-nominal credential ('Rachel Chen, CFA'). Additionally, 'CFA' may never be incorporated into a company name, domain, or logo (such as 'ChenCFA Wealth Advisors').

distractor_analysis.A: Promoting disciplined governance is standard business language, whereas misusing the trademark/adjective rules violates VII(B).
distractor_analysis.C: Ordinary descriptive terms like 'team' and 'wealth advisors' are completely permissible.

subtopic: Standard VII(B): Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program
module_title: Standard VII(B): Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Identify proper and improper references to CFA candidacy, membership, and the CFA designation under Standard VII(B)
question: Two years ago, Lucas Reed passed the CFA Level I exam. Due to demanding work travel, Reed has not registered for the Level II exam for the past two years and is not currently registered for any upcoming CFA exam sitting. On his LinkedIn profile headline and email signature, Reed writes: 'Lucas Reed, CFA Level II Candidate (CFA Level I).' Reed's profile violates Standard VII(B) because:

options.A: There is no partial 'CFA Level I' designation, and an individual may describe themselves as a CFA candidate only while actively registered for the next exam or awaiting results.
options.B: LinkedIn profiles are banned from mentioning passed CFA exam levels under any wording.
options.C: Only Level III passers may mention the CFA Program on public social networks.

explanation: Under Standard VII(B) (Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program), there is NO partial CFA designation ('CFA Level I' or 'CFA Level II' cannot follow a name). Furthermore, someone is a 'CFA candidate' ONLY if they have an active exam registration (or are awaiting exam results). Since Reed is not currently registered for Level II, calling himself a Level II Candidate and appending '(CFA Level I)' violates Standard VII(B).

distractor_analysis.B: Past passers who are not registered may still state factually in CV text: 'Passed Level I of the CFA Program in [year].'
distractor_analysis.C: Active Level I, II, and III candidates may accurately state their current candidacy status in factual prose.

subtopic: Standard VII(B): Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program
module_title: Standard VII(B): Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Identify proper and improper references to CFA candidacy, membership, and the CFA designation under Standard VII(B)
question: Sterling Global Asset Management's institutional pitchbook includes the following bullet point: 'Why Choose Sterling? Because 100% of our senior portfolio managers hold the Chartered Financial Analyst designation, our portfolios consistently generate superior risk-adjusted alpha and commit fewer judgment errors than non-charterholder competitors.' This marketing claim violates Standard VII(B) because it:

options.A: Spells out 'Chartered Financial Analyst' instead of abbreviating it as 'CFA.'
options.B: Discloses the percentage of portfolio managers holding the designation.
options.C: Exaggerates the meaning and implications of the CFA designation by claiming superior investment returns or lower error rates.

explanation: Under Standard VII(B) (Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program), members and firms must not misstate or exaggerate the meaning or implications of holding the CFA designation. While a firm may factually state that all senior managers hold the CFA charter and summarize what the program requires, claiming the charter guarantees superior investment performance, alpha, or fewer errors violates Standard VII(B).

distractor_analysis.A: Spelling out 'Chartered Financial Analyst' is completely valid and encouraged alongside proper usage rules.
distractor_analysis.B: Stating accurately what percentage of staff hold the CFA charter is factual and compliant.

subtopic: Standard VII(B): Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program
module_title: Standard VII(B): Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Identify proper and improper references to CFA candidacy, membership, and the CFA designation under Standard VII(B)
question: After earning her CFA charter six years ago, Priya Kapoor transitions from asset management to serve as corporate Treasurer of a manufacturing company. For two consecutive years, Kapoor forgets to pay her annual CFA Institute membership dues and skips submitting her annual Professional Conduct Statement (PCS). She nevertheless continues listing 'Priya Kapoor, CFA' on company investor press releases. Under Standard VII(B), Kapoor has:

options.A: Complied, because once earned, the right to use the CFA designation never lapses regardless of dues or PCS filing.
options.B: Violated Standard VII(B), because only active regular members current on annual dues and PCS filings are authorized to use the CFA designation.
options.C: Complied, provided she works outside the asset management industry.

explanation: Under Standard VII(B) (Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program) and CFA Institute Bylaws, the right to use the CFA designation is strictly contingent upon maintaining ACTIVE regular membership—including paying annual dues and submitting the annual Professional Conduct Statement (PCS). When membership lapses, the former charterholder must immediately cease displaying 'CFA' until reinstated.

distractor_analysis.A: While passing the three exams never expires, active authority to display the designation pauses immediately upon lapsed dues or missing PCS.
distractor_analysis.C: The active-membership rule applies regardless of whether the member works in corporate finance, banking, or asset management.

subtopic: Standard VII(B): Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program
module_title: Standard VII(B): Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Identify proper and improper references to CFA candidacy, membership, and the CFA designation under Standard VII(B)
question: Which of the following employee biographies in an investment firm's brochure complies fully with Standard VII(B) (Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program)?

options.A: 'Devon Brooks has passed Levels I and II of the CFA Program and is currently registered as a Level III candidate. Earning the CFA charter requires passing three comprehensive exams and committing annually to the CFA Institute Code and Standards.'
options.B: 'Devon Brooks, CFA Level III Candidate, will earn his CFA designation automatically next summer to enhance client returns.'
options.C: 'Devon Brooks is nearly a CFA, holding a Level II CFA credential that proves superior ethical conduct over non-members.'

explanation: Statement A adheres strictly to every rule under Standard VII(B): it states exam passage factually ('passed Levels I and II'), accurately states active registration ('currently registered as a Level III candidate'), avoids creating a partial designation after his name, and describes the charter's actual requirements (three exams plus annual Code commitment) without exaggerating future returns or moral superiority.

distractor_analysis.B: Appends a non-existent 'CFA Level III Candidate' title after the name, assumes guaranteed passing, and implies enhanced returns.
distractor_analysis.C: Uses 'CFA' as a noun ('nearly a CFA'), invents a partial 'Level II CFA credential,' and claims superior ethics over non-members.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Explain the objectives, firm-wide compliance, composite construction, and verification rules of GIPS
question: Global Horizon Partners manages both institutional equity strategies and high-yield municipal bond portfolios. Hoping to win an endowment equity mandate quickly, Horizon completes GIPS-compliant composite calculations strictly for its Global Equity division while ignoring GIPS accounting and composite rules in its fixed-income division. Horizon states in its RFP: 'Our Global Equity Composite is 100% GIPS-compliant.' Under GIPS, this claim is:

options.A: Permissible, provided the Global Equity division holds separate trading desks.
options.B: Permissible if fixed-income assets represent under 25% of total firm AUM.
options.C: Prohibited, because GIPS compliance can be claimed only on a firm-wide basis rather than for an individual composite or single division.

explanation: Under the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS), compliance is strictly an all-or-nothing, FIRM-WIDE commitment across a defined investment management firm holding itself out as a distinct business entity. A firm cannot claim GIPS compliance for a single composite, fund, or asset-class division while excluding the rest of the firm.

distractor_analysis.A: Unless the equity unit is formally defined and held out to the public as a distinct business entity under GIPS firm-definition rules, partial division claims are prohibited.
distractor_analysis.B: Asset percentage thresholds do not allow excluding a division from firm-wide GIPS compliance.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Explain the objectives, firm-wide compliance, composite construction, and verification rules of GIPS
question: When constructing a GIPS-compliant composite for a Large-Cap Core Equity strategy, which combination of portfolios MUST be included by the firm?

options.A: Only active surviving fee-paying accounts with assets above 1 million USD, plus three years of backtested simulated portfolios.
options.B: All actual, fee-paying, discretionary portfolios managed according to the Large-Cap Core Equity mandate—including terminated portfolios through their final full measurement period.
options.C: All discretionary and non-discretionary client accounts combined, excluding terminated accounts from prior years.

explanation: Under GIPS composite construction rules, a composite MUST include ALL actual, fee-paying, discretionary portfolios managed to the same investment mandate, objective, or strategy—including terminated portfolios up through their last full measurement period under management (to prevent survivorship bias). Non-discretionary portfolios and simulated/model accounts must NEVER be included.

distractor_analysis.A: Excluding smaller accounts or terminated accounts biases results, and simulated portfolios cannot be included in GIPS composites.
distractor_analysis.C: Non-discretionary accounts cannot enter GIPS composites, and excluding terminated accounts introduces survivorship bias.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Explain the objectives, firm-wide compliance, composite construction, and verification rules of GIPS
question: Crestline Capital has been managing discretionary institutional equity portfolios for nine full calendar years. This year, Crestline decides to adopt and claim compliance with the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS) for the first time. At a minimum, how many years of GIPS-compliant performance history must Crestline initially present, and how does the track record evolve thereafter?

options.A: Initially present at least 5 years of GIPS-compliant performance (or since inception if less than 5 years), then add one year annually until reaching a minimum 10-year compliant track record.
options.B: Initially present all 9 years immediately or wait until 10 full years exist before claiming compliance.
options.C: Initially present at least 3 years of GIPS-compliant performance and stop adding years once 5 years are reached.

explanation: Under GIPS presentation requirements, a firm initially claiming GIPS compliance must present at least 5 years of GIPS-compliant historical performance (or performance since the firm/composite inception date if less than 5 years old). After initial compliance, the firm must add one year of compliant performance each subsequent year until it reaches a minimum 10-year compliant track record.

distractor_analysis.B: A 9-year-old firm need only present a minimum of 5 compliant years at initial adoption, building up to 10 years over time.
distractor_analysis.C: The initial minimum is 5 years (not 3), and the ultimate minimum build-up target is 10 years (not 5).

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Explain the objectives, firm-wide compliance, composite construction, and verification rules of GIPS
question: Which statement accurately describes third-party verification under the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)?

options.A: GIPS verification is mandatory for every firm claiming compliance and may be performed internally by the firm's CFO.
options.B: Verification can be purchased exclusively for a single flagship composite without testing firm-wide composite policies.
options.C: Verification is voluntary, must be performed on a firm-wide basis by an independent third party, and does not certify the mathematical accuracy of any specific composite report.

explanation: Under GIPS, third-party verification is VOLUNTARY (though strongly encouraged), must be performed by an INDEPENDENT third party (never self-verified internally), and applies on a FIRM-WIDE basis. Importantly, verification assesses whether firm-wide policies/procedures comply with GIPS composite construction and calculation rules—it does NOT ensure the accuracy of any single specific composite presentation (unless an optional separate performance examination is also done).

distractor_analysis.A: Verification is voluntary (not mandatory) and cannot be performed by internal firm staff.
distractor_analysis.B: Verification cannot be restricted to one composite; it must cover firm-wide GIPS policies and processes.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Explain the objectives, firm-wide compliance, composite construction, and verification rules of GIPS
question: While preparing year-end GIPS performance reports for its Fixed Income Credit Composite, analyst Samuel Vance discovers that the firm values illiquid corporate private-placement bonds at historical amortized purchase cost rather than fair value, records bond coupon income on a cash-received basis instead of accrual accounting, and uses settlement-date accounting for trades. Which adjustment is required to maintain GIPS compliance?

options.A: Continue amortized historical cost for private placements while switching only coupon income to cash basis.
options.B: Value all assets at fair value, use trade-date accounting, and apply accrual accounting for fixed-income interest.
options.C: Use settlement-date accounting and market value solely at fiscal year-end.

explanation: GIPS calculation standards mandate that firms: (1) value all portfolio investments using FAIR VALUE (objective market value or fair-value estimation hierarchy, not amortized historical cost), (2) use TRADE-DATE accounting (mandatory for periods beginning on or after January 1, 2005), and (3) apply ACCRUAL accounting for fixed-income interest income (and accrual/ex-dividend accounting for equity dividends).

distractor_analysis.A: Amortized historical cost and cash-basis interest accounting violate GIPS fair-value and accrual rules.
distractor_analysis.C: Settlement-date accounting violates GIPS trade-date accounting mandates, and fair value applies at each valuation/external cash-flow point.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Explain the objectives, firm-wide compliance, composite construction, and verification rules of GIPS
question: Cascade Private Markets manages a closed-end, 10-year fixed-life private equity buyout fund in which the general partner holds full discretion over the timing and size of investor capital calls and cash distributions. When presenting GIPS-compliant performance to prospective limited partners, Cascade presents net and gross Money-Weighted Returns (since-inception IRR) rather than Time-Weighted Returns. Under GIPS, Cascade's return metric choice is:

options.A: Permissible, because GIPS allows Money-Weighted Returns when the manager controls external cash-flow timing and the vehicle is closed-end, fixed-life, or illiquid.
options.B: Prohibited, because GIPS mandates Time-Weighted Returns exclusively across every public and private asset class.
options.C: Prohibited, unless Cascade converts the private equity fund into a daily-liquidity mutual fund.

explanation: While GIPS requires Time-Weighted Returns (TWR) for most open-end public composites (to remove distortion from client-directed cash flows), GIPS expressly PERMITS Money-Weighted Returns (MWR / IRR) when the investment manager controls the timing of external cash flows AND the portfolio has closed-end, fixed-life, fixed-commitment, or predominantly illiquid private-market characteristics.

distractor_analysis.B: GIPS explicitly accommodates MWR for closed-end private market structures where managers control capital calls and distributions.
distractor_analysis.C: Private equity vehicles remain closed-end and properly use MWR under GIPS without converting to daily liquidity.

subtopic: Asset Manager Code of Professional Conduct
module_title: Asset Manager Code of Professional Conduct
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Apply the six core principles and key operational requirements of the CFA Institute Asset Manager Code
question: Under the CFA Institute Asset Manager Code of Professional Conduct (AMC), which governance failure at Zenith Global Funds most clearly violates the principle of Risk Management, Compliance, and Support?

options.A: Charging a tiered asset-based management fee disclosed in plain English in the prospectus.
options.B: Hiring an independent third-party pricing vendor for daily equity marks.
options.C: Allowing the Head of Equities Trading to simultaneously serve as Chief Risk Officer without an independent risk function or a tested Business Continuity Plan.

explanation: Under the Asset Manager Code's principle of Risk Management, Compliance, and Support, asset managers must maintain an independent risk-management function (separate from trading and investment decision-making), appoint an independent compliance officer, and establish a formal Business Continuity / Disaster Recovery Plan (BCP) that is regularly tested. Having the Head of Trading act as CRO without a tested BCP violates the AMC.

distractor_analysis.A: Disclosed tiered AUM fee schedules comply with the AMC Disclosures principle.
distractor_analysis.B: Using independent third-party pricing services is explicitly required best practice under AMC Performance and Valuation.

subtopic: Asset Manager Code of Professional Conduct
module_title: Asset Manager Code of Professional Conduct
subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
los: Apply the six core principles and key operational requirements of the CFA Institute Asset Manager Code
question: Vanguardia Credit Partners manages an open-end high-yield corporate credit fund holding 20% thinly traded distressed loans. To avoid recording a quarterly drawdown ahead of annual performance-fee crystallization, the lead portfolio manager overrides broker marks and sets quarter-end fair values internally without independent review. Under the CFA Institute Asset Manager Code (AMC), this practice violates:

options.A: Trading, because distressed loans must be traded exclusively on listed exchanges.
options.B: Performance and Valuation, which requires valuing portfolios fairly and accurately using independent third-party pricing sources whenever available.
options.C: Client Confidentiality, because third-party pricing reveals portfolio balances.

explanation: Under the Asset Manager Code's Performance and Valuation principle, managers must ensure client portfolios are valued fairly and accurately using objective market prices or independent third-party pricing sources, avoiding self-interested internal valuation overrides by portfolio managers whose fees depend on NAV.

distractor_analysis.A: Over-the-counter distressed loans are permissible if valued independently and fairly.
distractor_analysis.C: Obtaining objective pricing quotes from independent vendors does not breach client confidentiality.

question: A private wealth boutique claims adherence to the CFA Institute Asset Manager Code of Professional Conduct (AMC). During an operational review, an examiner discovers that the firm holds all client securities inside an unsegregated firm-affiliated ledger rather than an independent qualified custodian, and issues client portfolio holdings and fee reports only once per year. Under the AMC, these practices violate required standards for:

options.A: Safeguarding client assets via independent custody/segregation and providing client reporting at least quarterly (with fee/conflict disclosures at least annually).
options.B: Limiting equity portfolio turnover below 20% annually.
options.C: Requiring every client to sign weekly trade confirmations.

explanation: Under the Asset Manager Code (Risk Management, Compliance, and Support & Disclosures), managers must protect client assets by utilizing independent custodians and segregating client accounts where feasible, provide clear client account reporting at least QUARTERLY, and disclose fee structures, soft-dollar policies, proxy policies, and conflicts at least ANNUALLY.

distractor_analysis.B: The AMC sets no arbitrary 20% turnover ceiling when trades are suitable and achieve best execution.
distractor_analysis.C: Quarterly reporting—not weekly client trade signatures—is the AMC reporting floor.

question: Which statement best describes the relationship between the CFA Institute Asset Manager Code of Professional Conduct (AMC) and the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct?

options.A: The AMC replaces the individual Code and Standards once a charterholder becomes a Chief Investment Officer.
options.B: The AMC is a voluntary firm-level ethical framework specifically tailored to investment management organizations, complementing the individual obligations of the Code and Standards.
options.C: Adopting the AMC is mandatory for all firms employing at least one CFA candidate and automatically confers GIPS compliance.

explanation: Whereas the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct govern INDIVIDUAL members and candidates, the Asset Manager Code of Professional Conduct (AMC) establishes voluntary, firm-level ethical and operational standards specifically for INVESTMENT ORGANIZATIONS (asset managers) across six core areas: Loyalty to Clients, Investment Process and Actions, Trading, Risk Management/Compliance/Support, Performance and Valuation, and Disclosures.

distractor_analysis.A: Individual CFA members and CIOs remain permanently bound by the Code and Standards regardless of whether their firm adopts the AMC.
distractor_analysis.C: AMC adoption is voluntary (not mandatory upon hiring a candidate), and it is distinct from claiming GIPS compliance.
